candidates.title: Nebius tests the neocloud playbook with $40 billion in planned spending
candidates.snippet: Nebius plans to fund its $40 billion AI infrastructure expansion through customer prepayments and loans, even as delays at a Microsoft data center raise questions about its financing model.
candidates.text:
In its third-quarter earnings call Thursday, the neocloud company Nebius laid out $40 billion in planned spending for 2027, far more than Wall Street had expected. It’s an ambitious plan, but it rests on a string of planned projects that are already starting to show cracks.
Nebius plans to fund the buildout by relying on customer pre-payments and loans backed by customer contracts — essentially using the future value of its data centers to finance their construction. But that can be a risky strategy if those projects get bogged down by delays or cancellations.
“Building at this scale is hard, and delays are part of our industry right now,” CEO Arkady Volozh said during Thursday’s earnings call. “We are not immune.”
The earnings announcement comes on the heels of reports that Microsoft is cooling on neocloud deals that aren’t delivering on time. That’s a problem for companies like Nebius, whose financing strategy is becoming more dependent on repayments. Because if it can’t get to capacity on time, it will keep piling on costs while revenues slip.
One of Nebius’ largest customers is Microsoft, which is paying for AI computing capacity at a Vineland, New Jersey, data center that is now months behind schedule. Nebius’ contract with Microsoft is worth up to $19.4 billion, but it’s already letting deadlines slip. Only just over half of the Microsoft capacity is now planned for delivery by the end of the year, with the rest coming in Q2 2027.
The delay is because DataOne, the third-party operator of the site, “decided to wind down the temporary generation faster than it was expected,” according to Andrey Korolenko, chief product and infrastructure officer, as the site switches over to Bloom Energy fuel cells.
Still, that transition wasn’t entirely by choice. In August , the investigative site Floodlight identified at least 45 natural gas generators in operation at the DataOne site, even though it had not received any permits for operating gas generators. New Jersey regulators fined the DataOne facility $1.1 million in response, finding that the use of the generators violated federal law.
DataOne is also facing a noise-complaint lawsuit from nearby residents over a constant humming noise allegedly emitted by the data center.
According to Nebius’ summary of its Microsoft contract, Microsoft can terminate affected service after a grace period if dates are missed and no alternative capacity is offered. The tranches were originally meant to be deployed in 2025 and 2026, so a Q2 2027 delivery date falls well beyond that window. The contract also includes financial penalties for late delivery.
Nebius said that Microsoft “has been part of the planning process.” Nebius did not say whether Microsoft has agreed to the new dates, but Microsoft has not publicly canceled anything.
TechCrunch has reached out to Nebius, Microsoft, and DataOne for comment.
On the call, Marc Boroditsky, Nebius’s chief revenue officer, said the company’s deals with Microsoft and Meta both came with significant prepayment, which arrived long before delivery. But Bloomberg reported last week that Microsoft is tightening oversight on projects run by third parties, including Nebius, IREN, and Nscale, and debating whether it’s worth signing new agreements. Microsoft also sent employees to the site in New Jersey, per Bloomberg.
In its own quarterly earnings report, Microsoft noted that its capex spend was lower than expected due to third-party delays. The company is clearly not above pulling back from planned agreements where its partner doesn’t meet its share of the bargain. Bloomberg also reported that Microsoft won’t use an option to more than double its Nscale agreement for a Texas data center and recently stopped being an anchor customer for Nscale’s planned Essex site after power delays.
Nebius says the delays it faces are coming from sites it doesn’t control, with the data centers it is building itself coming online on time or ahead of schedule. Those, Nebius says, will supply most of its new capacity from 2027. New deals signed in Q3 came with prepayments that more than cover the cost of building capacity behind them, says Boroditsky. Nebius ended the quarter with $7.4 billion in cash.
Total prepayments plus asset-backed financing of investment-grade contracts are expected to cover up to 85% of the $40 to $45 billion 2027 capex spend. CFO Maria Del Dado Alonso Sanchez named Microsoft and Meta as contracts that can be financed this way. Boroditsky also said Nebius could “tap prepayments to shore up any additional cash requirements.”
Nebius forecast 2027 revenue of $12 to $13 billion, and said it expects to break even on a pre-tax basis by the fourth quarter.
Nebius reported third-quarter revenue of $981 million, up 571% from a year earlier. Roughly a third of that was a one-time payment tied to a new partnership model. Nebius cut its 2026 revenue forecast by $200 million to $3 billion, citing delays to third-party sites like New Jersey. Shares ended the day down 17%.

candidates.title: Hugging Face CEO vows to keep fighting for open source AI after Jensen Huang’s exit
candidates.snippet: Hugging Face's CEO pledged to keep fighting for open source AI after Huang's exit, raising questions about Nvidia's $12.9 billion acquisition.
candidates.text:
Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue briefly commented on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s departure on Thursday, calling it a “really sad day.” Nvidia had announced its plan to acquire the platform for open source AI models in September for $12.9 billion, making it the second-largest acquisition in the company’s history, just behind that of chipmaker Groq’s assets for $20 billion in December 2025.
“This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!,” Delangue wrote on X.
This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened. It’s a really sad day!
But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go! — clem 🤗 (@ClementDelangue) November 12, 2026
The post is interesting as it implies that Huang’s departure is potentially worrying to open source advocates, and he’s attempting to offer reassurance.
As Nvidia’s CEO, Huang was known as a strong advocate for open source AI and open-weight models, which is why there could be concerns about how a company that’s no longer under his leadership will now approach this space.
After Nvidia announced its plans to acquire Hugging Face, the U.S. Department of Justice began making inquiries about how the deal would impact competition in the AI market, Reuters reported in October . While Nvidia pledged that the platform would preserve open support, it would also allow the company to control a major distribution channel for AI models.
The Hugging Face deal is still scheduled to close in the first half of 2027. Requests for further comment on the deal status and whether Hugging Face has spoken yet with Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress were not returned.
Huang’s advocacy for open source and open-weight AI has long extended beyond Hugging Face. In July, the CEO published an AI policy letter as his first-ever post on the social network X . The letter, which was signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, Hugging Face, IBM, Palantir, and others, urged the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models. It said models that “anyone can download, inspect, modify, and run on their own infrastructure” are an important part of the AI ecosystem because they make AI “more accessible, adaptable, and widely available.”
Huang also wrote that open-weight models expand access to the AI economy, strengthen competition, and give customers greater control, as they know they won’t become locked into a single provider. “Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty,” his post on X stated.
For my first post, I’m sharing a letter @NVIDIA signed on why open models matter.
AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country.
Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty.… pic.twitter.com/t02bi51N4C — Jensen Huang (@JensenHuang) July 24, 2026
In August, Nvidia also announced a $6 billion deal with the coding startup Poolside to help build out an open AI ecosystem in the U.S. to help the country compete against Chinese companies like DeepSeek and Kimi K3, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time. Last month, Nvidia expanded its Nemotron family of open-weight models with a large 120-billion-parameter model for agents used by the enterprise as well as with two new lightweight Bolt models that run on PCs.
Earlier this year, Huang promoted open source AI during his January keynote address at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas, noting that open source models have “really revolutionized artificial intelligence.”

Nvidia Rival Fractile Hits $7B Valuation With $720M AI Chip Funding
British AI chip startup Fractile raises $720M at a $7B valuation, backed by Google, BlackRock and the UK government ahead of its 2027 chip launch.
Emir Abyazov 2 min read
12 November 2026, 01:14 PM Prefer us on Google
Key takeaways
Fractile raises $720 million at $7 billion valuation
Google and UK government back Nvidia challenger
First commercial AI chips expected in 2027
British AI chip startup Fractile has raised $720 million at a $7 billion valuation, attracting backing from Google-linked investors, BlackRock and the UK government as competition intensifies to develop alternatives to Nvidia's artificial intelligence processors.
The November 11 Series C round was co-led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed and Redpoint. Alphabet's CapitalG, DST Global, Balderton and several other investors also participated.
The UK government's announcement confirmed investments from its Sovereign AI fund and the British Business Bank, describing the financing as part of Britain's strategy to develop domestic semiconductor capabilities.
Fractile's $720M Funding Targets Nvidia's AI Chip Dominance
Founded in 2022 by Walter Goodwin, Fractile is developing processors specifically designed for AI inference, the process of generating responses after a model has been trained.
Unlike conventional AI accelerators, Fractile's architecture places dynamic random-access memory directly above processing components, seeking to reduce the delays caused by moving data between memory and computing units.
The company argues that memory bandwidth increasingly limits AI performance, particularly as reasoning models and autonomous agents generate longer outputs.
Its technology could eventually challenge Nvidia's dominant position in AI inference, although commercial performance remains unproven.
The financing arrives as Google expands its exposure to alternative AI chip developers, including a recently disclosed $548 million Qualcomm stake.
Other companies are pursuing similar opportunities through custom AI accelerators , as cloud providers seek more specialized computing hardware.
Google and UK Government Back Fractile's Expansion
Fractile's investors include major technology-focused funds alongside British public institutions, reflecting growing demand for alternatives to foreign semiconductor suppliers.
The British government said the investment would help the company expand its engineering operations across London and Bristol while strengthening domestic AI infrastructure.
The round also comes amid Nvidia's continued investment in AI chip research , where rapid innovation remains essential to protecting its competitive advantage.
However, Fractile faces significant execution challenges.
The company expects to introduce its first commercial chip in 2027, meaning its current valuation largely reflects investor expectations rather than established product revenue.
Can Fractile Challenge Nvidia in AI Inference?
Fractile is entering a competitive market that includes established semiconductor companies and emerging developers such as Groq and Etched.
Nvidia has already pursued inference technology investments to strengthen its position as AI workloads expand beyond model training.
Fractile must demonstrate that its architecture delivers meaningful improvements in speed, energy consumption and cost under real-world conditions.
Its financing also reflects the broader AI infrastructure investment boom , where substantial capital is flowing into companies before their technologies achieve commercial scale.

SoftBank Bets approximately $5.4 Billion on Swiss Robotics as Foreign Capital Influx Deepens
Add preferred source
Japan's SoftBank Group is pouring large sums into Switzerland's robotics industry, agreeing to acquire ABB's robotics division for $5.4 billion and investing $200 million in Gravis Robotics, a construction-robotics startup spun out of ETH Zurich. Foreign investors account for 88% of capital in deep-tech funding rounds of $100 million or more, and 43% of Swiss scale-ups are university or research-institute spin-offs. However, the share of Swiss investors in later-stage rounds has fallen from 27% to 13%, with limited mass-production experience and the flight of domestic capital cited as challenges at the growth stage.
Key Elements
SoftBank Group ABB Gravis Robotics ETH Zurich Deep Tech Nation Switzerland Switzerland Global Enterprise (S-GE) Neura Robotics Swissmem Swisscom Ventures EPFL
Japan's SoftBank Group is injecting large sums into Switzerland's robotics industry in quick succession. After agreeing to acquire the robotics division of Swiss automation company ABB for $5.4 billion (~7.2 trillion won), SoftBank in August invested $200 million (~270 billion won) in Gravis Robotics, a construction-robotics startup spun out of ETH Zurich. Gravis said the round was the largest Series A investment ever in the construction-robotics sector.
SoftBank's string of bets encapsulates the recent surge of foreign capital into Swiss deep-tech companies. According to the "Swiss Scale-up Report 2026" published this year by Deep Tech Nation Switzerland, foreign investors accounted for 88% of the capital in deep-tech funding rounds that raised $100 million or more. In effect, Swiss companies are raising their growth capital from abroad.
Speaking at a robotics and automation event hosted by Switzerland Global Enterprise (S-GE) in Zurich, Switzerland, on the 11th (local time), investment and industry officials agreed that foreign capital looks at the depth of research accumulated before a company's founding rather than its short history. They explained that technology and intellectual property (IP) built up over years in university labs, combined with research talent from around the world, heighten investment appeal.
Alexandre Meldem, head of international communications at Deep Tech Nation Switzerland, said, "Even if a company was only recently founded, there may be 10 years of science behind it," adding, "Switzerland is a relatively stable country with a predictable policy environment, which is an advantage because it allows investors to look 10 years ahead."
Indeed, research institutions are the key starting point for deep-tech companies in Switzerland. Of 265 Swiss scale-ups, 115—or 43%—are spin-offs from universities or research institutes. Forty-two came from ETH and 41 from EPFL. Some foreign robotics companies have even set up bases in Zurich directly to tap the research ecosystem. German robotics company Neura Robotics is developing core hardware technology for humanoid robots in Zurich.
Urs Laupi, chief strategy officer (CSO) of Neura Robotics, cited cooperation with ETH, physical AI research talent, and the capital environment as reasons for choosing Zurich as its base. "Switzerland has a solid knowledge base in the field of physical AI," he said, stressing that "we can combine world-class Swiss research capabilities with Germany's industrialization capabilities."
Switzerland also operates a separate intermediate stage to validate research results before they are applied on actual factory floors. The Swiss Cobotics Competence Center (S3C) at the Switzerland Innovation Park Biel/Bienne supports proof-of-concept (PoC) testing of robotics technology before companies invest in automation equipment, and once validation is complete, hands the results to system integrators and others to connect them to industrialization.
The competitiveness of Swiss robotics companies was not built on university research alone. As the precision machinery and automation industries developed long ago, a manufacturing base for applying lab technology to real industry was built alongside them. A Chinese venture capital (VC) official also cited precision machinery technology and the manufacturing base supporting it as reasons for paying attention to Swiss robotics companies.
Roger Sonderegger, industry sector manager at Swissmem, the Swiss association for the mechanical, electrical, and metal industries, explained that "high labor costs accelerated automation in Swiss manufacturing," adding that "from the 1970s and 1980s, automation was adopted to cope with high production costs, and competitiveness was built around precision machinery and high-value-added products rather than mass production."

Norwest: $4 Billion Fund Expands Global Multi-Stage Investment Strategy
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 11:42 AM
Norwest: $4 Billion Fund Expands Global Multi-Stage Investment Strategy
Norwest has closed Norwest 18, a $4 billion global investment fund that will back venture and growth equity opportunities across technology, healthcare, and consumer markets. The vehicle is the largest fund in the firm’s 65-year history and increases its total capital under management to $18 billion.
Norwest will deploy the new fund across the United States, India, and Israel, continuing a strategy that spans early-stage venture investments through later-stage growth equity. The firm said this flexible approach allows it to begin working with companies at different stages and continue supporting them as their capital requirements and operating priorities evolve.
Since launching Norwest 17 in April 2024, the firm has completed more than 87 investments and worked with over 30 portfolio companies on liquidity events. Initial public offerings during that period included Amagi Media Labs, BillionToOne, MBX Biosciences, Omada Health, and Swiggy.
Strategic acquisitions involving Norwest-backed businesses included EQT’s acquisition of Avetta, Luminate Capital Partners’ purchase of AbsenceSoft, Gilead Sciences’ acquisition of Ouro Medicines, Salesforce’s purchase of Qualified, Pinterest’s acquisition of tvScientific, and ServiceNow’s purchase of Veza.
Norwest 18 will maintain the firm’s primary sector focus while increasing its exposure to emerging categories. Areas of interest include next-generation financial infrastructure, physical and voice AI, agentic cybersecurity, technology-enabled industrial and aerospace businesses, and healthcare AI.
Recent financial infrastructure investments include Beltic, Rain, and Stablecore. Norwest has also backed Coval, Generalist AI, and LlamaIndex in intelligent AI systems; Above Security, ORION Security, Red Access, and Zenity in cybersecurity; and East Range Group, Padmini VNA, JJG Aerospace, and Raghu Vamsi Aerospace Group in industrial and aerospace markets.
Healthcare investments include Infinx, Matchpoint Therapeutics, Rezo Therapeutics, Tokaido Health, and Vitalize Care. These businesses are applying AI to drug discovery, clinical and administrative workflows, healthcare access, and care-team productivity.
Beyond financing, Norwest provides portfolio companies with operating support and strategic guidance. The firm has doubled the size of its Senior Advisor Network, added operating executives, and launched the Norwest Operator Collective and Norwest Kinetic. These resources are intended to help management teams address technology, go-to-market, talent, and organizational challenges.
Since its founding in 1961, Norwest has invested in more than 750 companies and currently works with over 275 venture and growth equity portfolio companies. Its offices are in Menlo Park, San Francisco, Mumbai, and Tel Aviv.
KEY QUOTES
“Building and scaling a company has never been a linear journey, and today that journey is becoming more complex. Companies are staying private longer, scaling across markets, and navigating critical decisions around technology, talent, and growth. Capital is only one part of what they need. Our role is to be a long-term partner and bring the experience, networks, and resources that can help leadership teams make those decisions with confidence.”
Jeff Crowe, Senior Managing Partner at Norwest
“Markets and technology change, but what has remained consistent at Norwest is our ability to identify strong businesses, invest patiently, and stay closely aligned with the founders, CEOs, and leadership teams we partner with. Our multi-stage strategy allows us to meet companies where they are and continue supporting them as they grow. Norwest 18 gives us even greater flexibility to do that across sectors, stages, and geographies.”
Jon Kossow, Managing Partner at Norwest

By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 2:21 PM
Pfizer: Up To $1.5 Billion Funding Agreement With Blackstone Life Sciences To Advance Monthly GLP-1 Obesity Drug
Pfizer and Blackstone Life Sciences have entered into a strategic funding agreement under which funds managed by Blackstone will provide up to $1.5 billion through 2028 to support the clinical development of berobenatide, Pfizer’s investigational monthly GLP-1 receptor agonist for chronic weight management and obesity-related conditions.
The agreement will help Pfizer advance its obesity drug development program while maintaining financial flexibility to invest in other therapeutic areas. In exchange for its funding commitment, Blackstone will become eligible for milestone-based payments tied to U.S. regulatory approval and commercial performance.
Berobenatide is being developed as a potential first-in-class monthly injectable GLP-1 receptor agonist peptide. Pfizer is evaluating the treatment for chronic weight management and obesity-related conditions, including knee osteoarthritis and obstructive sleep apnea.
The transaction represents a significant investment in Pfizer’s cardiometabolic pipeline as the pharmaceutical company advances a broad portfolio of investigational obesity therapies.
How The $1.5 Billion Funding Agreement Works
Under the agreement, Blackstone-managed funds will cover up to $1.5 billion in development expenses associated with berobenatide through 2028.
In return, Blackstone will be eligible to receive payments if the drug achieves specified regulatory and commercial milestones.
These payments are contingent on U.S. regulatory approval of monthly injectable berobenatide monotherapy for chronic weight management and the achievement of certain sales targets.
Any milestone payments earned by Blackstone would be distributed over multiple years.
The structure allows Pfizer to obtain external funding for a major clinical development program without selling ownership or commercial rights to the investigational medicine.
Pfizer will retain full operational control and decision-making authority over berobenatide, including its clinical development strategy.
The agreement also does not provide Blackstone with an ownership interest in the drug.
Funds managed by Blackstone’s perpetual private equity strategy, BXPE, will participate alongside funds managed by Blackstone Life Sciences.
The arrangement illustrates an alternative approach to financing pharmaceutical research, in which investment firms provide capital to support clinical development in exchange for payments linked to future milestones.
For Pfizer, the agreement provides an opportunity to share development costs while retaining control over a potentially important pipeline asset.
Berobenatide Targets Monthly GLP-1 Treatment
Berobenatide is an investigational GLP-1 receptor agonist peptide being studied for chronic weight management and related medical conditions.
GLP-1 receptor agonists act on biological pathways involved in appetite regulation, blood glucose control, and other metabolic processes.
Existing treatments in this drug class have established a significant market for obesity and metabolic disease therapies.
Pfizer is developing berobenatide as a potential monthly injectable treatment, which could offer a different administration schedule from therapies requiring more frequent dosing.
The company is pursuing an extensive clinical development program to evaluate the drug’s safety and effectiveness.
Pfizer plans to advance more than 20 clinical trials involving obesity and associated medical conditions during 2026.
These include 10 ongoing and planned Phase 3 trials for berobenatide.
The studies are intended to evaluate the treatment across chronic weight management and obesity-related conditions.
Pfizer is also investigating berobenatide in combination with other investigational therapies.
The company is studying combinations involving nutrient-stimulated hormone peptides, including amylin analogs.
These approaches are part of Pfizer’s broader strategy to develop treatments that act on multiple biological pathways associated with weight regulation and metabolic health.
Berobenatide remains investigational, and its safety, effectiveness, and potential approval have not yet been established by regulators.
Expanding Pfizer’s Cardiometabolic Pipeline
Pfizer is positioning berobenatide as a central component of its cardiometabolic research and development portfolio.
The company is evaluating the therapy both as a standalone treatment and in combination with other investigational medicines.
Its development strategy extends beyond weight loss to conditions associated with obesity.
Knee osteoarthritis and obstructive sleep apnea are among the conditions included in the clinical research program.
Obesity can contribute to a range of medical complications, creating opportunities for therapies that improve weight management and potentially address related health outcomes.
Pfizer’s clinical program is intended to generate evidence about berobenatide’s potential across different patient populations and treatment settings.
The agreement with Blackstone provides additional resources to support this work through 2028.
Pfizer said the funding arrangement will also allow it to maintain capacity for investment across its broader pharmaceutical pipeline.
By supplementing internal research spending with external capital, the company aims to pursue multiple development priorities simultaneously.

Rowan Digital Infrastructure: $1.5 Billion In New Financing To Accelerate 5.5 GW Hyperscale Data Center Pipeline
By Amit Chowdhry

Rowan Digital Infrastructure: $1.5 Billion In New Financing To Accelerate 5.5 GW Hyperscale Data Center Pipeline
Rowan Digital Infrastructure, a Denver-based developer of hyperscale data center campuses, has secured more than $1.5 billion in new corporate financing capacity to accelerate development of its 5.5-gigawatt project pipeline across the United States. The financing includes a $600 million expansion of its holding company term loan led by Apterra Infrastructure Capital, along with a new $590 million revolving credit facility and a $355 million letter of credit facility led by Citibank.
The transactions provide Rowan with additional financing flexibility to secure land, obtain power commitments, purchase equipment, and advance early-stage development activities across its portfolio of hyperscale data center projects.
With the latest transactions, Rowan has secured more than $8 billion in financing from over 40 lenders during the past 18 months.
The company’s development pipeline includes multiple large-scale data center campuses designed to support major technology companies and hyperscale computing operators.
Rowan has already contracted more than 1.2 gigawatts of capacity with major technology customers.
The additional corporate financing is intended to help the company accelerate the development of new facilities while maintaining access to capital across multiple projects.
$600 Million Term Loan Expansion
Rowan expanded its existing holding company credit facility by $600 million, increasing the total facility size to $900 million.
The original $300 million facility was established in September 2025 to support early-stage development activities.
Apterra Infrastructure Capital served as lead arranger for the expanded financing.
The additional term loan capacity provides Rowan with resources to support project development before individual campuses reach the construction financing stage.
These activities can include land acquisition, infrastructure planning, engineering, permitting, and coordination with electricity providers.
Early-stage financing is particularly important in hyperscale data center development because projects can require significant capital commitments before construction begins.
Rowan’s expanded corporate facility allows the company to pursue additional opportunities while progressing existing projects through development.
New $945 Million Credit Facilities Led By Citibank
In addition to the term loan expansion, Rowan established two new corporate credit facilities totaling $945 million.
The financing consists of a $590 million revolving credit facility and a $355 million letter of credit facility.
Citibank served as lead left arranger and administrative agent for both facilities.
The revolving credit arrangement provides Rowan with access to liquidity that can be borrowed, repaid, and borrowed again as its project pipeline develops.
This structure is intended to reduce the need for the company to obtain separate financing for every new development site.
The letter of credit facility provides financial support for obligations associated with project development.
These can include utility interconnection deposits, equipment vendor commitments, and other collateral requirements.
Letters of credit can help developers satisfy certain financial obligations without immediately posting equivalent amounts of cash.
Both facilities include provisions allowing for potential future expansion.
Subject to applicable conditions, Rowan may increase the revolving credit facility to as much as $2 billion and the letter of credit facility to as much as $1 billion.
These potential increases are not part of the initially committed $945 million.
The lender syndicate includes Citibank, Mizuho Bank, MUFG Bank, Goldman Sachs Bank USA, Societe Generale, Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, and Huntington National Bank.
Several participating banks have previously supported Rowan’s project-level financing transactions.
Supporting A 5.5 GW Data Center Development Pipeline
Rowan is developing a portfolio of hyperscale data center campuses across multiple U.S. markets.
Its pipeline totals approximately 5.5 gigawatts of planned capacity, with more than 1.2 gigawatts already contracted.
The company specializes in build-to-suit infrastructure designed to support hyperscale operators requiring substantial computing capacity.
These facilities typically require extensive electrical infrastructure, specialized cooling systems, and significant investment in equipment and construction.
Access to electricity and the ability to deliver operational capacity quickly have become increasingly important factors in data center development.
Rowan’s business model emphasizes securing strategic locations and coordinating infrastructure development to meet customer requirements.
The new financing will help support these activities across the company’s growing portfolio.
Rowan is actively developing campuses ranging from approximately 300 megawatts to more than one gigawatt in capacity.
The company’s broader strategy is supported by investment partnerships with Quinbrook and Blackstone.
More Than $8 Billion In Recent Financing Activity
The latest corporate financing transactions build on several major project-level funding milestones completed during 2026.
In May, Rowan secured approximately $2.9 billion for its 300-megawatt Temple data center campus.
The transaction represented the largest financing in the company’s history and was completed under Rowan’s Green Finance Framework.
Earlier in February, the company obtained $550 million in construction financing for its 300-megawatt Cinco campus in Medina County, Texas.
Rowan also secured $925 million for the third phase of its Bauxite development in Frederick County, Maryland.

SAN FRANCISCO , Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, we're announcing that we've raised $1B in a Series A, led by Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital, with participation from Battery Ventures, Doerr Capital, Gil & Co, Google, M13, Pear VC, and S32, among other new and existing investors.
We believe making AI R&D more accessible is the most direct path to AI that solves humanity's most pressing problems across science and technology. We're building tools to democratize frontier AI R&D and help put it within reach of every scientist and engineer.
Over the past three weeks, we've shared our first results, and they point to the same shift: when agents do the hands-on work, the size of your team stops limiting what you can build. One researcher, working with agents, pretrained Mirendil-Base , a competitive coding model, from scratch in 3.5 months with less than $10M in compute. We then post-trained it into Fern , which holds up to 10M tokens of context, enough for days of an agent's work. And Lor , now in private beta, brings this way of working to everyone else: hundreds of agents writing code and running experiments for days at a time. Mirendil runs on Lor every day.
This round lets us go further, toward a world where one person can take on what used to need a team, a team what used to need an institution, and we can help accelerate science and technology in a more direct way than we've done before.
We're still a small team with a singular focus. If you want to help make frontier AI R&D accessible to everyone, join us . If you'd like to build with Mirendil, we'd like to hear from you at [email protected] .

CKX Lands: $1 Billion Brad Jacobs Investment To Launch New Public Company Platform
By Amit Chowdhry
Yesterday at 7:15 AM
CKX Lands: $1 Billion Brad Jacobs Investment To Launch New Public Company Platform
Jacobs Private Equity II and minority co-investors have agreed to invest $1 billion in CKX Lands, creating a public company platform that Brad Jacobs plans to use to build a business in an industry that has not yet been selected.
Jacobs Private Equity will provide $900 million, while co-investors led by HRTG Partners will contribute $100 million. Jacobs Private Equity will hold a majority interest following the transaction.
Brad Jacobs will become chairman and chief executive officer of CKX while continuing to serve in the same roles at building products distributor QXO.
CKX will be renamed and operate as a separate public company. Before closing, it will convert from a Louisiana corporation to a Delaware corporation, complete a holding-company reorganization, and conduct a 4.1744380-for-1 reverse stock split.
The investors will receive voting convertible perpetual preferred shares convertible into approximately 219 million common shares at $4.57 per post-split share. They will also receive warrants to purchase approximately 219 million additional shares at exercise prices ranging from $4.57 to $13.70.
Following closing and before warrant exercises, Jacobs Private Equity and its co-investors will own approximately 99.78% of the company on a fully convertible and exchangeable basis.
CKX will declare a $20.8 million cash dividend, equal to $10.1312 per existing share, before the transaction closes. Existing investors will retain exposure to CKX’s land business while participating in the potential future company.
The board unanimously approved the investment, and shareholders representing approximately 28% of voting power agreed to support it. Completion is expected in early 2027, subject to shareholder approval and other conditions.
Jacobs has founded or led eight billion-dollar or multibillion-dollar companies and participated in approximately 500 acquisitions. The new platform would become his ninth company.
KEY QUOTES
“I love building multibillion-dollar market leaders, and this $1 billion investment marks the launch of my ninth company. After concluding my chairmanships of XPO, GXO, and RXO last year, I now have the capacity to create this new venture while continuing to lead QXO to its massive potential.”
Brad Jacobs, Founder of Jacobs Private Equity II
“We believe this investment will create compelling outcomes for our stakeholders, including the opportunity for our stockholders to receive a substantial upfront cash payment as part of a $20.8 million dividend. We expect our stockholders will benefit from retaining the value of our existing land business while also participating in the potential upside of Brad Jacobs’ future plans for the company.”
William Gray Stream, President of CKX Lands

This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here .
It was another big week for AI-related startup financings. Mirendil , a developer of agentic AI for R&D, led the pack with a $1 billion series A, followed by Mercor , which secured $750 million to connect AI developers with human experts.
Overall, the vast majority of this week’s largest rounds were AI-related, though we did see some biotech, fintech and enterprise software in the mix.
1. Mirendil , $1B, AI for R&D: Mirendil, a developer of agentic AI technology for research and development, secured $1 billion in a Series A funding. Kleiner Perkins and Clearlake Capital led the round for the San Francisco-based startup.
2. Mercor , $750M, human-led AI training: Mercor, a platform that connects AI developers with human experts for model training and evaluation, raised $750 million in Series D funding. The round, backed by a long list of venture investors, set a $20 billion valuation for the San Francisco-based company, which was founded less than four years ago.
3. Torus , $500M, AI infrastructure: Salt Lake City-based Torus, a manufacturer of distributed power and compute infrastructure, announced a $500 million growth financing led by Magnetar Capital . It also introduced a product called Foundry, described as modular AI infrastructure for inference compute.
4. (tied) Path Robotics , $300M, AI for manufacturing: Path Robotics, a developer of physical AI technology for robotics and manufacturing, with initial expertise in welding, picked up $300 million in Series E financing. Georgian led the round, which set a $2.45 billion valuation for the Columbus, Ohio-based company.
4. (tied) LangChain , $300M, agentic AI: LangChain, developer of a platform to run, improve and govern AI agents, closed on $300 million in Series C funding at a $3 billion valuation. CapitalG led the round for the 4-year-old, San Francisco-based company.
6. Nominal , $240M, hardware engineering tools: Nominal, a developer of intelligence tools for hardware engineering, raised $240 million at a $3 billion valuation. Lightspeed Venture Partners and Insight Partners led the round for the Austin-based startup.
7. (tied) Imprint , $130M, fintech: Imprint, a payments, loyalty and customer intelligence platform for brands, landed $130 million in new funding at a $1.9 billion valuation. Khosla Ventures led the financing for the 6-year-old, New York-based company.
7. (tied) Mavria , $130M, AI infrastructure: Mavria, a startup focused on standardizing how AI infrastructure is developed, built and deployed, launched publicly and said it has raised $130 million in pre-seed and seed funding to date. Its latest round, led by Paradigm , sets a $1 billion valuation for the startup, whose founders formerly worked at the U.S. Department of Energy .
9. (tied) Delix Therapeutics , $100M, biotech: Delix Therapeutics, a startup that says it has “reverse-engineered and optimized psychedelics” to develop treatments for psychiatric and psychological disorders, closed on $100 million in Series C funding. Johnson & Johnson Innovation and SV Health Investors ’ Dementia Discovery Fund led the financing for the Bedford, Massachusetts-based company.
9. (tied) Rox , $100M, sales automation: San Francisco-based Rox, developer of an AI revenue agent for enterprise sales, announced a $100 million Series B financing led by General Catalyst and March Capital .
9. (tied) Databento , $100M, financial market data: Databento, a finance data platform, secured $100 million in Series C funding at a $1.1 billion valuation. Fifth Down Capital led the round for the Salt Lake City-based company.

We tracked the largest announced rounds in the Crunchbase database that were raised by U.S.-based companies for the period of Nov. 7-13, 2026. Although most announced rounds are in the database, there may be a small time lag, as some rounds are reported late in the week.

RENO, Nev. , Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Positron AI , the AI inference hardware company built to make generative AI dramatically cheaper and more energy-efficient, today announced it has been named to the inaugural 2026 AI 100 , the definitive ranking of the top 100 private AI companies in the world, published by Newcomer in collaboration with Bessemer Venture Partners .
The inaugural AI 100 recognizes leading private companies driving innovation across the AI ecosystem. Positron's inclusion reflects its progress in bringing purpose-built inference technology to market as growing AI adoption drives demand for more cost- and energy-efficient infrastructure.
"We're honored to be recognized among the companies shaping the future of AI," said Mitesh Agrawal, CEO of Positron AI. "Making AI inference profitable, scalable and accessible takes advanced technology and a business and supply chain built to serve some of the world's largest technology companies. Positron combines deep semiconductor and systems expertise with customer-driven development and investor backing to position us for growth. I'm proud of the business we're building as we serve customers today and develop our next generation of technology, and grateful to our team, customers, partners and investors for their support."
Positron's recognition follows a series of major company milestones. In September, the company announced an $875 million Series C financing at a $5 billion valuation to accelerate development of its next-generation Asimov silicon, ramp production of Titan and expand manufacturing capacity. Positron has also deployed more than 50 racks of Atlas, its first-generation inference system, at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. Most recently, the company announced a partnership with General Compute, which is purchasing Atlas systems and has committed to adopting Titan to support next-generation AI workloads.
The inaugural AI 100 evaluated nominated companies and recognized category leaders across four factors: market leadership (35%), estimated valuation (30%), operating metrics (20%), and people & culture (15%). Only independent AI companies that have not had a majority strategic or private equity M&A transaction or a public listing were eligible. Honorees span foundation models, AI infrastructure and compute, developer tools and agents, AI apps, vertical AI, security, physical AI and robotics, and deeptech and AI for science.
"The artificial intelligence startup set plays by its own rules: there are upstarts with unprecedented revenue growth, companies profiting off of seemingly insatiable inference spending, highly valued speculative research labs, and wildly ambitious robotics companies. These AI native startups are already reshaping the global economy. With our friends at Bessemer, we rethought what matters for the AI age, bringing together the most promising startups harnessing foundation models to transform our digital and physical world," said Eric Newcomer, founder of Newcomer.
"The AI 100 puts a spotlight on the top 100 companies driving the AI economy forward, built by a generation of founders moving at a speed and scale we've never seen before. We're already seeing that exponential value creation play out across infra, AI applications, and physical AI. The remarkable part is that it's still early: this inaugural cohort is just the starting point, a natural evolution of our decade-long Cloud 100 franchise," said Byron Deeter, partner at Bessemer Venture Partners.
The inaugural AI 100 is published at ai100.newcomer.co , and was unveiled live onstage at the Cerebral Valley AI Summit in San Francisco.
About Positron AI
Positron AI builds hardware and software to make AI inference dramatically cheaper and more energy efficient. The company's shipping product, Atlas, is deployed at hyperscaler scale today, and its next-generation custom silicon, Asimov, tapes out in late 2026 with production in the second half of 2027. Asimov powers Titan, a multi-terabyte-memory inference system for long-context and next-generation AI workloads. Positron's energy-efficient architecture allows its systems to be deployed in air-cooled or liquid-cooled data centers at varying rack densities, without dependence on constrained HBM or CoWoS supply chains. Mercor Raises $750 Million in Series D at $20 Billion Valuation
The round includes an employee tender, but Mercor did not disclose how much goes to share sales or new company capital. The company plans to expand AI evaluation and post-training work for businesses.
By John Kim
Published Nov 11, 2026, 4:06 PM EST
Save Share Three miniature task stations under warm studio light / TokenPost.ai
Mercor detailed a broader enterprise AI evaluation and post-training push in a Nov. 10 announcement of a $750 million Series D that values the company at $20 billion.
The round includes an employee tender, but Mercor did not disclose how much of the $750 million is tied to employees selling shares or how much will go to the company as new capital. The company plans to invest in research and infrastructure for evaluations and post-training, along with additional environments where AI agents can practice complex workflows.
Over the past two years, Mercor has developed systems for training and assessing frontier AI models. Its enterprise evaluations use companies’ actual workflows and requirements, giving businesses a way to assess models against tasks shaped around their operations.
More than five million experts work through Mercor’s network and receive payment for training frontier AI models. “Every job in the economy will need its own agents that can perform tasks reliably and efficiently,” Mercor co-founder and CEO Brendan Foody said.
Investors named in the round include Benchmark, Felicis, Fundomo, funds managed by Apollo affiliates, G Squared, General Catalyst, Glade Brook Capital, NVIDIA, Salesforce, Sapphire Ventures, StepStone Group, XTX Ventures and Zoom.
Mercor’s previous announced financing was a $350 million Series C at a $10 billion valuation on Oct. 27, 2025. In July, the company announced plans to acquire Deeptune, which builds training environments for reinforcement learning. Deeptune’s team had recreated hundreds of enterprise applications over two years.

Insider Brief
Ukraine-founded defense technology company Uforce raised $700 million in Series A funding at a $6 billion valuation to expand production of autonomous military systems for Ukraine and allied nations.

Ukraine-founded defense technology company Uforce has raised $700 million in Series A funding at a $6 billion valuation to expand production of autonomous military systems for Ukraine and allied nations.
The round was co-led by Valor Equity Partners and the UK National Wealth Fund, with participation from the U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund, according to Uforce . Other investors included Menlo Ventures , Xantium and Hiro Capital, while existing backers Shield Capital , Ballistic Ventures , Lakestar and Squadra increased their stakes.
Headquartered in London, with major operations in Kyiv and Washington, Uforce develops uncrewed systems for air, land and sea operations, along with AI software for coordinating and controlling them. The company said the funding will support manufacturing expansion across the United States, Europe, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East, while maintaining production and supplies for Ukrainian forces despite continued attacks in Ukraine.
Expanding Autonomous Defense Production
Uforce plans to increase production and research and development across four product families: MAGURA uncrewed surface vessels, NEMESIS aerial drones, LIUT ground vehicles and PREDATOR turret systems.
The company also anticipates working with partners in allied countries to adapt existing maritime and automotive manufacturing facilities for defense production.
Uforce recently announced a partnership with ReconCraft to expand U.S. manufacturing of its Maritime Autonomous Guard Unmanned Robotic Apparatus (MAGURA) vessels. It also plans to build on relationships within NATO and Joint Expeditionary Force networks and continue participating as a founding member of the EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance.
CEO Oleg Rogynskyy said the financing will help increase production for Ukraine while providing allied nations with autonomous systems they can deploy, integrate and maintain.
“The war in Ukraine has shown that in an increasingly volatile world, effective defense requires systems that can keep improving as threats change,” noted Rogynskyy. “Governments and the technology ecosystem need to come together to develop cost-effective, interoperable, and autonomous platforms that are ready to fight now, and can evolve to meet future needs.”
Investment Supports Ukrainian Operations
The U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund’s participation will specifically support Uforce’s operations in Ukraine, including staffing, research and development, and new products. The fund was established jointly by the United States and Ukraine to attract investment into reconstruction, economic development and strategic industries.
Uforce also announced that retired Gen. Christopher G. Cavoli, former NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe and a partner at Valor Equity Partners, will join its board of directors.

UFORCE, the Ukrainian company behind the MAGURA sea drones , has raised €630 million ($700 million) . The round was co-led by Valor Equity Partners and the UK National Wealth Fund (NWF). New investors include the US–Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund (URIF), Menlo Ventures, Xantium and Hiro Capital. Existing backers Shield Capital, Ballistic Ventures, Lakestar and Squadra increased their stakes.
Worker.ai , a company operating system for small businesses backed by Veeam founder Ratmir Timashev, has acquired DeltaGen , a Prague-based startup that builds real-time voice AI. The financial terms of the deal were not disclosed. All three of DeltaGen’s founders are moving to Worker. DeltaGen’s team of around 10 people will stay in Prague.
Vilnius-based Biomatter , which uses AI to design enzymes, has raised an oversubscribed €16.2 million ($18 million) Series A . The round was led by Astanor , with existing investors UVC Partners, Inventure and Metaplanet also taking part. Founded in 2018, Biomatter designs enzymes by starting from the chemical reaction a customer needs .
Czech medtech startup Kardi AI has raised €5.3 million in a Series A round led by German healthtech fund Callisto Health. According to the company, this is the largest round a Czech medtech startup has raised to date. Česká spořitelna and Slovenská sporiteňa joined through their corporate venture programmes. Earlier backers BrightCap Ventures, Purple Ventures, DEPO Ventures and Garage Angels also put in money. After the round, Kardi AI is valued at €23 million.
Hedepy, the Prague-based online therapy platform operating in nine European countries, has secured €4 million in venture debt from Orbit Capital to fund acquisitions and expand into clinical care and AI tools — aiming to consolidate Europe’s fragmented mental health market.
Valkyrie Dynamics, the Ukrainian-Lithuanian defense startup building a 100-gram radar seeker that lets low-cost drones intercept targets through cloud and fog, raised €1 million in a pre-seed round led by Paris-based venture studio Hexa — developed and field-tested alongside operators in Kyiv.
Romanian edtech company Kinderpedia , which has developed a management and communication platform for schools and kindergartens, has secured a €500,000 investment from BCR Seed Starter , the corporate venture capital arm of BCR. The investment completes Kinderpedia’s €2.7 million funding round , led by Polish fund Simpact Ventures, with participation from existing investors Early Game Ventures and ROCA X.
Italian-founded legal AI company Lexroom has launched lex , an AI-powered personal assistant for lawyers accessible through WhatsApp, just two months after acquiring Bulgarian legal tech company Praven Intelekt . The new product aims to help legal professionals manage administrative tasks, conduct legal research, and prepare documents directly through a messaging app.
New funds launching
BlackPeak Capital , a private equity firm that invests growth equity in Southeast Europe, has announced the first close of BlackPeak Southeast Europe Growth Equity Fund II (BPSEEF II) at €125 million . That is almost as much as the €126 million its first fund raised in total. The Luxembourg-domiciled fund is targeting €150 million, has a hard cap of €200 million, and expects to hold its final close in 2027. BPSEEF II will invest between €7 million and €20 million per deal in fast-growing companies. Its primary markets are Bulgaria, Romania, Croatia, Slovenia and Serbia, and it may also invest opportunistically in Poland, Hungary, Slovakia, the Baltic states and other Western Balkan countries.
Polish venture capital firm Bitspiration VC is preparing to launch a new €50 million biotech fund , supported by investors including Snowflake co-founder Marcin Żukowski and Tomasz Onyszko, co-founder of Predica and CTO of Morning Brew. The firm has already secured investor commitments for a first close of €15–20 million, scheduled for November.

candidates.text:
Robotics
Agile Robots Raises $500 Million From SoftBank and Nvidia
Jakob Steinschaden , co-produced by AI 12. November 2026, 07:43
© Agile Robots
Set Trending Topics as a preferred source on Google.
While Europe is still debating whether humanoid robots will ever make it onto the factory floor, SoftBank and Nvidia are putting half a billion dollars on the table for it: Agile Robots, the Munich-based robotics company, has just closed a funding round of $500 million (about €450 million). The round lifts its valuation to $8.5 billion (about €7.6 billion), the German news agency dpa reported.
The Round at a Glance
Hard Facts
Agile Robots
Valuation
$8.5 billion (about €7.6 billion)
Amount
$500 million (about €450 million)
Stage
not disclosed (most recently a Series C in 2021)
Investors
SoftBank Group (lead), Nvidia, Hitachi, T.Capital
Total raised to date
about $2 billion (about €1.8 billion)
Existing investors
including SoftBank Vision Fund and Xiaomi
SoftBank is not a new backer: The Japanese company already led the $220 million Series C in 2021 that made Agile Robots a unicorn. How much SoftBank is contributing this time is not known. The other names are no surprise, either. Nvidia had already announced its investment in Agile Robots in Berlin in October, and the company has been working since September on physical A.I. for manufacturing with Hitachi, which is investing through its venture arm. T.Capital is the investment company of Deutsche Telekom.
What the Money Is For
Zhaopeng Chen, the founder and chief executive, wants to use the capital mainly for three things: entering the U.S. market, new industrial applications and manufacturing in Bavaria. Early this year, Agile Robots opened a new plant in Fürstenfeldbruck, near Munich, that is designed for up to 10,000 humanoid robots a year. The company is taking the technology straight from the lab into industrial series production, Mr. Chen said.
According to The New York Times , the round is also meant to prepare for a possible initial public offering. There is no timetable for that. Physical A.I. could help Europe close its gap with the United States and China in artificial intelligence, Mr. Chen argued there.
What Agile Robots Does
Agile Robots was started in 2018 as a spinoff of the German Aerospace Center, known as DLR, in Oberpfaffenhofen. Mr. Chen had worked there on, among other things, especially sensitive robot hands. Today the company sells almost everything that moves in a factory: robot arms, robot hands and grippers, driverless transport systems, complete production cells and the humanoid robot Agile ONE, along with its own control platform.
By its own account, Agile Robots employs more than 3,500 people at more than 25 sites, over 2,000 of them in development. More than 20,000 automation solutions are installed worldwide, it says, and it holds more than 650 patents. Its customers include large companies in the automotive, consumer electronics, health care and logistics industries.
Agile Robots has also grown through acquisitions, including that of Franka Robotics, a Munich maker of robot arms. For A.I., the company relies on partners: A research partnership with Google DeepMind has been running since the spring, followed in October by a humanoid platform based on Nvidia’s robotics models and a logistics project with Audi. Besides Germany, the company also manufactures in China and India, and its earlier investors include Xiaomi, the Chinese electronics company.
SoftBank Is Buying Its Way Into Robotics
For SoftBank, Agile Robots is one piece of a bigger bet. Masayoshi Son’s company agreed in 2025 to acquire ABB’s robotics division for $5.4 billion (about €4.9 billion) and has taken a large stake in Skild AI, an American start-up working on a universal A.I. model for robots. In that strategy, ABB supplies the bodies and Skild AI the brain.
The Competition
Money is currently flowing into many robot makers. In Germany, Neura Robotics , of Metzingen, raised up to $1.4 billion (about €1.3 billion) in the summer, from investors including Tether, Amazon and, likewise, Nvidia. The Munich start-up RobCo has become a unicorn. In the United States, Apptronik raised $520 million (about €467 million) at a valuation of about $5 billion, and then there are Figure, 1X and Tesla with Optimus, as well as Unitree of China.
High Valuation, Few Numbers
What stands behind the $8.5 billion valuation remains open: Agile Robots does not disclose revenue or earnings, and the number of installed solutions says little about how many humanoid robots are actually in use. In June, moreover, there had still been talk of a round of about $800 million. Why it has now become $500 million is not known.
There is also skepticism in principle. At the invest.austria conference, Nikolaus Keuth of EY recently spoke of a “big graveyard of pilot projects” in humanoid robotics: The technology is often not ready yet, expectations are too high, and without a real business case one is only chasing a fantasy. The panel there agreed that the race for the factory floor is still open.

SoftBank Leads $500 Million Funding Round for Agile Robots in Germany
By: Asia Business Outlook Team | Thursday, 12 November 2026
Japanese investment group SoftBank has led a US$500 million funding round in German robotics company Agile Robots , valuing the company at US$8.5 billion.
The funding round also saw participation from semiconductor company Nvidia , Japanese technology firm Hitachi and T. Capital.
The investment comes as interest in artificial intelligence and robotics continues to grow, with more companies looking to use these technologies in manufacturing and other industries.
Agile Robots plans to use the funds to expand its business in the United States, increase production in Germany and develop new industrial applications.
The company is looking to benefit from the growing demand for automation technology across manufacturing, logistics and other sectors. The investment is also expected to help it strengthen its position in the global robotics market .
Key Highlights
SoftBank Leads $500 Million Funding Round in German Robotics Firm Agile Robots
Agile Robots Reaches $8.5 Billion Valuation After SoftBank-Led Investment
Nvidia and Hitachi Join SoftBank in $500 Million Investment in Agile Robots
SoftBank and Nvidia Support Agile Robots' Expansion
Founded in 2018 by researchers from the German Aerospace Center, Agile Robots develops robotic systems that combine artificial intelligence with advanced hardware. Its products include industrial robotic arms , robotic hands, autonomous transport systems and humanoid robots used for different industrial applications.
The company has more than 3,500 employees across over 25 locations worldwide. It also says that more than 20,000 of its automation solutions are currently in use globally. Agile Robots holds over 650 patents related to its technology.
With the latest investment, the company has raised approximately US$2 billion since its establishment. SoftBank had previously led a US$220 million Series C funding round in Agile Robots in 2021, helping it expand its operations.
Nvidia's participation is another important part of the deal. The chipmaker has been increasing its investments and partnerships in robotics as it looks to expand the use of AI beyond computers and data centres. This includes physical AI , which allows machines to understand their surroundings and carry out tasks in the real world.
Agile Robots has also partnered with Google DeepMind to improve the capabilities of its robotic systems. The collaboration is aimed at developing robots that can perform more complex tasks in industrial settings.
Company Plans to Increase Production in Germany
Agile Robots will use the new funding to expand its operations in the United States and increase its manufacturing capacity in Germany. It also plans to develop more applications for its robotic systems as manufacturers look for ways to improve productivity and reduce manual work.
Earlier this year, the company opened a manufacturing facility in Fürstenfeldbruck, near Munich. The facility is designed to produce up to 10,000 humanoid robots annually. This will help Agile Robots increase production and prepare for growing demand.
The company sees humanoid robots as an important part of the future of industrial automation . Designed to work in spaces built for humans, these robots could be used in factories, warehouses and other workplaces to handle different tasks.
The investment also reflects SoftBank's growing interest in artificial intelligence and robotics. The Japanese group has been backing companies developing technologies that combine AI software with physical machines. Its agreement to acquire ABB's robotics division for US$5.4 billion is another example of its interest in the sector.
Agile Robots is entering a competitive market, with several companies investing in humanoid robots and industrial automation. As manufacturers look to improve efficiency and reduce operating costs, demand for these technologies is expected to increase.

Its ability to turn these investments into commercial growth will be important as competition in the global robotics market continues to increase.

Germany’s Agile Robots Raises $500M in Series F Funding to Expand Physical AI Production
By Greg Bock · 12 November 2026 · 2 min read
Insider Brief
German robotics company Agile Robots raised $500 million in Series F funding at an $8.5 billion valuation to expand physical AI production capacity and strengthen its international operations.
The SoftBank Group-led round included Nvidia, Hitachi Group and T.Capital, bringing Agile Robots’ total invested capital to $2 billion.
Agile Robots reports 20,000 deployed industrial robotic solutions and operates a German facility capable of producing up to 10,000 legged and wheeled humanoid robots annually.
German robotics company Agile Robots has raised $500 million in Series F funding at an $8.5 billion valuation to increase manufacturing capacity and expand its physical AI business internationally.
The SoftBank Group -led round included Nvidia , Hitachi Group, through Hitachi and Hitachi Ventures , and T.Capital . According to Agile Robots , the financing brings its total invested capital to $2 billion.
The Munich-based company plans to use the funding to strengthen its presence in the United States, expand production capacity, including in Germany , and develop additional robotics applications.
Agile Robots makes humanoid and mobile robots , robotic arms and hands , along with the AI models and software used to control them. Its customers include companies in the automotive, consumer electronics, healthcare and service industries.
“Physical AI will fundamentally change how the world builds, moves and makes things,” founder and CEO . Zhaopeng Chen said. “Our vision is intelligent robots working alongside people in factories and warehouses everywhere, and Agile Robots is determined to lead that shift. We bring Physical AI out of the lab and into industrial production, across logistics, automotive, electronics and manufacturing.”
Expanding Industrial Production
The company reported that it has deployed 20,000 industrial robotic solutions since its founding, including systems used in automotive manufacturing, consumer electronics and logistics. Earlier this year, Agile Robots opened a manufacturing facility in Fürstenfeldbruck, near Munich, with the capacity to produce up to 10,000 legged and wheeled humanoid robots annually.
Agile Robots was founded in 2018 as a spin-off from the German Aerospace Center (DLR), initially focusing on bringing robotics research into industrial applications.
The company now has more than 2,000 research and development specialists and over 650 patents, according to the announcement. Its portfolio includes Franka Robotics, an AI robotics research platform, and Krause Automation, an industrial deployment specialist recently acquired from thyssenkrupp.

VulcanForms announces $500M financing agreement

VulcanForms plans to build three factories by the end of 2027 including one in Massachusetts, fueled by a $500 million financing deal the company announced Thursday.
“Factory No. 4” is planned for Massachusetts, according to VulcanForms CEO Kevin Kassekert, who confirmed the company also plans to double its workforce to approximately 1,000 by the end of 2027.
The financing, led by J.P. Morgan and Apollo-managed funds, supports three additional factories by the metal parts manufacturer that has existing operations in Newburyport and two in Devens where it is adding 1 million square-feet of manufacturing space .
VulcanForms, a pioneer in advanced digital manufacturing, said it plans to use the funding to accelerate the next phase of American industrial production.
Backed by multibillion-dollar commercial programs across critical industries, VulcanForms said it is expanding to meet growing customer demand, marking a milestone in the company’s transition from breakthrough manufacturing technology to industrial-scale production, according to a press release.
ADVERTISEMENT
As American industries seek to strengthen domestic production and reduce dependence on fragmented global supply chains, the challenge extends beyond technological innovation to manufacturing complex, high-performance components at the scale, speed and cost required to compete globally, the company said.
VulcanForms is addressing the challenge through a fully integrated digital manufacturing platform that combines metal additive manufacturing, precision machining, automation and physical AI.
By unifying traditionally fragmented production processes, the company is establishing a new model for producing critical components competitively in the U.S., it says.
Kevin Kassekert, CEO of VulcanForms Photo I Courtesy VulcanForms
“America cannot lead the next industrial revolution if we can’t manufacture what we invent,” Kassekert said. “For too long, breakthrough technologies developed here have been manufactured overseas.
ADVERTISEMENT
“VulcanForms is proving we can change that by turning American innovation into industrial-scale production and demonstrating that the U.S. can not only compete, but also win on the global stage. We’re proud to work with J.P. Morgan and Apollo on helping to build America’s industrial future at home.”
VulcanForms uses advanced 3D printing and machining to make complex metal parts for industries like aerospace, medical and defense. The company has presented itself as part of an effort to reshore manufacturing and to secure domestic supply chains.
The firm was awarded $21.26 million in tax credits from the Massachusetts Economic Assistance Coordinating Council to support the construction of a 1-million-square-foot advanced manufacturing facility in Devens.
The expansion is part of an effort to establish a multi-facility VulcanForms campus in Devens, according to ConnectCRE.com .
ADVERTISEMENT
VulcanForms has secured multibillion-dollar commercial programs spanning medical devices, consumer products, aerospace, defense, space and industrial markets, demonstrating significant demand for its integrated manufacturing platform.
VulcanForms was founded out of MIT in 2015. The firm works with clients to design parts and manufacture them in its own facilities, seeking to minimize sourcing of raw materials from overseas.
The company has secured multibillion-dollar commercial programs across critical industries, raising over $1 billion in funding since its launch including $220 million in January that included a contribution from Florida-based 1789 Capital , a venture capital firm whose partners include Donald Trump Jr.

candidates.text:
Source: Nikki / Wikimedia Commons
Exus Renewables North America said Thursday it closed $345 million in senior secured holding company financing led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives, money the company says will go toward construction and new U.S. wind, solar and battery projects.
The check is another in a run of company financings and project deals, not a map of which turbines or panels get the cash. Exus framed the close against rising U.S. electricity demand and described itself as an independent owner, developer and operator of utility-scale renewable energy and storage.
What the Money Is For
Exus said the financing will support construction costs and development across its growing U.S. portfolio of wind, solar and battery storage assets. The announcement does not name the projects that will draw on the facility or split the dollars among those three technologies.
President and CEO Jim Spencer said the financing lets the company keep its momentum going. He also said Goldman Sachs Alternatives' support reflects confidence in Exus and gives it flexibility to build projects and bring generation online, including work already underway and a deeper pipeline.
Vikas Agrawal, managing director and co-head of Energy Transition Climate Credit at Goldman Sachs Alternatives, said Exus has a strong platform for developing and operating utility-scale renewable projects. "We're pleased to support its continued investment in new energy infrastructure," he said, tying that support to growing U.S. electricity demand.
A Larger Company-Reported Book
Exus reported more than 800 megawatts operating or under construction and a total portfolio exceeding 6 gigawatts. Those are company figures, not an outside audit of nameplate capacity.
The comparison that is on the record is Exus' own July 22, 2025 financing announcement. Then, the company reported more than 5 gigawatts in its total portfolio and 764 megawatts operating or under construction, alongside $308.2 million in financing for the 185-megawatt Zia Solar portfolio in New Mexico and the 169-megawatt Keystone wind portfolio in Pennsylvania.
From that July 2025 snapshot to Thursday's release, the company-reported operating-or-under-construction figure moved from 764 megawatts to more than 800, and the total portfolio from over 5 gigawatts to more than 6. Exus also said it is expanding its operational footprint to meet growing national energy needs, with work that includes developing, repowering and managing renewable assets.
Separate Deals, Not One Stack
This holding-company financing sits beside other Exus transactions that the available reporting treats as separate. pv magazine USA reported in January that Exus had closed a $400 million senior secured corporate credit facility tied to a 4.5-gigawatt pipeline. Nothing in the Thursday announcement establishes whether that facility is still outstanding or how it relates to the $345 million.
Project-level money has also moved on its own track. On Sept. 22, Exus said it had completed the Highland North and Cambria wind repower projects in Cambria County, Pennsylvania, and that construction was financed through roughly $356 million led by KeyBanc Capital Markets. A week later, on Sept. 29, Exus and ibV Energy Partners announced that Exus had acquired four solar projects totaling 715 megawatts-peak.
Those deals show a company adding and rebuilding capacity in named places — Cambria County wind, a New Mexico solar book, Pennsylvania wind — while Thursday's $345 million is described only at the holding-company level.
Demand, Offices and the Close
Exus put the financing in a market it describes as tight on power. In the Cambria County release, the company said demand for clean power from data centers and other large energy users keeps climbing across that region. Nationally, a Jan. 13 Energy Information Administration release forecast the strongest four-year growth in U.S. electricity demand since 2000, fueled by data centers, and said solar would supply the largest increase in power generation, up a forecast 21% in both 2026 and 2027 after almost 70 gigawatts of new capacity. That is a forecast, not a reading of what Exus will actually build.
The company said it has more than 110 employees operating from offices in Pittsburgh, New York, Albuquerque and Connecticut. PEI Global Partners was financial advisor to Exus. Latham & Watkins LLP was legal counsel to Exus, and Vinson & Elkins LLP was legal counsel to Goldman Sachs Alternatives.
What Thursday actually puts on the table is $345 million of senior secured holding-company financing, led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives, for construction costs and new wind, solar and storage development — with the project list still unstated.

The Institutional Infrastructure Battery Fund (IIBF) is launching as an infrastructure investment fund for institutional investors, specifically focused on large-scale battery energy storage systems (BESS) in Germany. At launch, the fund has already secured its first two storage projects in central Germany under purchase agreements and has an identified project pipeline representing an investment volume of more than €300 million.
As renewable energy deployment progresses, large-scale battery storage systems are becoming an important component in stabilizing the German electricity grid and balancing volatile generation peaks. The IIBF translates this structural infrastructure need into an investment profile tailored to regulated institutional investors: the fund invests in a diversified portfolio of large-scale battery storage projects in Germany that are ready to build or close to their commercial operation date (COD) and holds them for the long term following acquisition. Early-stage project development and permitting risks therefore remain outside the fund.
Clearly defined responsibilities: institutional investment management and European energy trading expertise
The IIBF is built on a clearly defined division of responsibilities between two established specialists in their respective markets:
Investment management, underwriting and structuring by 2IP: Institutional Investment Partners (2IP) is responsible for investment management, transaction underwriting and institutional fund structuring. As the storage facilities are held throughout the fund's term, pre-acquisition due diligence is particularly important: 2IP assesses each transaction against clearly defined risk, financial viability and cash flow criteria, incorporates contractual security mechanisms and provides ongoing oversight through its portfolio and investment management.
Market access, asset management, software and energy trading by Second Foundation: As one of Europe's major technology-driven energy traders, the Second Foundation Group manages the energy-related and technological value chain surrounding the storage facilities. This ranges from direct project access and commercial and technical asset management of the facilities, through proprietary control and monitoring software, to high-frequency trading of capacity in the European electricity and balancing markets.
Contractually underpinned base distributions with additional market upside
The IIBF's income model is designed to cushion downside exposure to the volatility typical of electricity markets while also harnessing it for the portfolio. The core of the fund's income consists of long-term contractual usage fees (lease payments) for making the storage facilities available. Contractual advance payments and additional security mechanisms support the predictability of regular distributions to investors.
In addition, performance-linked remuneration components allow investors to participate directly in Second Foundation's trading performance in the electricity and balancing markets. As the majority of projected total income is generated continuously from ongoing operations during the holding period, the overall return depends only to a limited extent on eventual disposal proceeds at the end of the fund's term – significantly reducing terminal value risk.
