candidates.text:
Four of six deals are reported in Chicago, and the region is experiencing the latest funding activity in the form of investments in AI infrastructure and financial services.
According to StartMidwest’s funding roundup , $213.5 million was raised in six deals by Midwest startups and financial technology companies during the week ending Nov. 6, with two $100 million rounds accounting for almost all the capital.
Ocient, an AI infrastructure firm in Chicago, and Erebor Bank, which is based in Columbus, Ohio, were the leaders of the activity. The remaining included health care technology, artificial intelligence and fintech firms, reflecting the diversity of sectors that are being invested in all over the region.
The headline figure, however, requires some qualification: Erebor Bank’s $100 million investment from Japan’s SBI Holdings was announced as a planned commitment, not a completed financing round. The difference is important in evaluating the amount of capital that actually has flowed to companies in the Midwest.
The biggest round up to date was Ocient’s $100 million Series C , which was announced on November 5. The investment, led by BOKA Capital and OCA Ventures, totals $260 million for the Chicago firm. Other investors who were on board included existing investors Greycroft, In-Q-Tel, Blue Bear Capital, Buoyant Ventures, PSP Growth, Pritzker Group Venture Capital and Eron Wolf. Dallas Venture Capital joined as a new investor.
Ocient is a company that creates data analytics and AI solutions for enterprises dealing with vast amounts of data. The new investment will allow it to continue developing its OcientAIQ solutions that enable enterprises to deploy AI agents and analytics in petabyte-scale data environments.
Reliable, governed data is becoming a key infrastructure need as businesses delve into agentic AI systems that can analyze information and execute tasks. Ocient claims its solution can be used for data governance along with high-performance data analytics, enabling AI agents and analysts to ask questions about the data in a customer’s environment.
The company anticipates that its revenue will more than triple in 2026 due to the demand of customers with growing and high-volume data sets. This projection is not a financial result but an estimate by Ocient.
The second $100 million was from a digital bank called Erebor Bank, based in Columbus, Ohio, which offers services to companies in fields such as artificial intelligence, robotics and advanced manufacturing, defense, and energy. The timing of the completion of the investment was not mentioned in the funding roundup, but SBI Holdings revealed its plan to invest $100 million .
Four of the six transactions were in Chicago. In addition to Ocient, medical technology firm Focused Medical Technologies, a treatment developer for pulmonary embolism, secured $6 million in investment, including two medical technology strategic investors and UCM Ventures. The University of Chicago startup is targeting the funds for product development, manufacturing and setting up for a pivotal study in the United States.
Consumer insights firm QualSights raised $5 million in funding, led by Duo Partners. The company employs smart sensors and a consumer application and AI analytics to provide a better understanding of how humans use physical products. The funding came with the appointment of Prasanna Pitale as Chief Executive.
Fifth Star Funds and Chicago Early Growth Ventures joined Izou Partners as the lead investors in an oversubscribed $2.5 million pre-seed round for healthcare technology company CareLumi. Its software will track AI-powered and automated workflows in healthcare delivery systems, starting with provider credentialing and payer enrollment.
Minneapolis-based Duome capped the list with a capital investment from Great Lakes Credit Union. The company is connecting with credit unions to assist homebuyers who meet the qualifications to acquire homes using a co-investment approach.
The four of the deals occurred in Chicago, Columbus, and Minneapolis, each had one deal. The sector split also indicates that the regions aren’t just focused on traditional software startups – the financial services, health care, and AI infrastructure sectors are also included.
Nevertheless, the weekly total was very skewed. The two $100 million deals made up about 94% of the total $213.5 million reported, with the remaining four deals making up a much smaller portion of the total.
The numbers indicate ongoing investor interest in tackling complex challenges in infrastructure and industry-specific issues for the Midwest startup ecosystem. However, the size disparity between these large financing announcements and the smaller rounds at the early stage also poses a question for the region: Is it possible to reliably get capital to startups at various stages of development?

Blue J Announces $176M in Funding at $700M Valuation to Scale AI Tax Research Agent
By James Dargan · 12 November 2026 · 1 min read
Toronto-based Blue J, which builds AI software for tax research, has secured US$176 million in a round led by Baltimore’s JMI Equity, valuing the company at US$700 million. Existing investors Oak HC/FT, Sapphire Ventures and Intrepid Growth Partners also took part.
Nearly US$100 million will go towards buying shares from employees and early investors, with the remaining US$80 million funding the commercialisation of Blue J’s new agent product and expansion into the UK, its third market after the US and Canada.
Founded in 2015 by University of Toronto law professor Benjamin Alarie and two colleagues, Blue J answers complex tax questions in seconds with source citations. Alarie rebuilt the product around large language models after ChatGPT arrived in 2022, and says accuracy has risen from roughly 50% in early versions to more than 95%.
The deal comes just over a year after a US$122 million round in August 2025. Recurring revenue has since grown 165% to the mid-eight-figure range, and client firms have increased from fewer than 100 three years ago to more than 6,500.
JMI principal Jack Duane said the firm had tracked Blue J for years, heard strongly positive customer feedback and considers the product extremely difficult to replicate thanks to its proprietary data and domain expertise.

Ondas Posts Record $167.5 Million Q3 Revenue, Raises 2026 Outlook
1 min read

Ondas reported third-quarter 2026 revenue of $167.5 million, up 100% sequentially and more than 16-fold year over year. Gross profit was $36.5 million, with a GAAP gross margin of 21.8%, while net loss was $64.7 million. Formed Ondas Sentinel, combining DZYNE Technologies and World View under unified leadership to advance U.S. defense programs and the development, production, and deployment of defense technologies.

Advanced customer programs and product deployments, including counter-drone protection at major sports venues, a U.S. Army follow-on task order, the Digital Bat program, and the first flight of Blitz Block 3. Ondas also opened a training, testing, and flight-operations hub in Springfield, Ohio.

MaxCyte: $151.8 Million Akron Bio Acquisition Expands Cell Therapy Platform
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 11:44 AM
MaxCyte: $151.8 Million Akron Bio Acquisition Expands Cell Therapy Platform
MaxCyte has agreed to acquire Akron BioProducts from affiliates of Arcline Investment Management for $151.8 million. The transaction is expected to close before the end of 2026, subject to customary conditions.
Akron Bio supplies Good Manufacturing Practice-grade reagents and ancillary materials used across cell therapy manufacturing. Its products include cytokines, growth factors, human plasma-derived materials, specialty media, and other consumables.
The acquisition will expand MaxCyte beyond its historical focus on nonviral cell engineering. Akron’s products are used in both viral and nonviral workflows at stages ranging from cell expansion through cryopreservation.
The combined company’s technologies are incorporated into five commercially approved therapies and support more than 100 clinical programs. Both businesses maintain drug master files referenced in customers’ regulatory submissions, creating long-term connections to validated manufacturing processes.
Akron is expected to produce approximately $28 million in 2026 revenue and between $7 million and $8 million of EBITDA. MaxCyte expects the acquisition to nearly double its revenue base, increase recurring consumables revenue, and accelerate its path toward profitability.
The companies have limited customer overlap despite serving similar biopharmaceutical markets. MaxCyte therefore expects to use its commercial infrastructure to introduce Akron products to additional customers and pursue cross-selling opportunities.
The buyer projects that Akron’s positive cash flow will help reduce the combined company’s annual cash burn to less than $10 million in 2027. MaxCyte expects to hold approximately $40 million to $45 million of cash when the transaction closes.
The consideration consists of $105 million in cash, subject to adjustments, 20,639,733 MaxCyte shares valued at approximately $26.8 million, and $20 million of guaranteed deferred payments. The deferred amount will be paid in two $10 million installments in January 2028 and January 2029.
MaxCyte has also secured a credit facility of up to $75 million from MidCap Financial, consisting of a $55 million term loan and a $20 million revolver. It plans to draw $20 million from the term loan and $2 million from the revolver at closing.
Akron will continue operating under its existing brand, with its management team and employees remaining part of the combined organization.
KEY QUOTES
“The acquisition of Akron marks an exciting new chapter for MaxCyte. This acquisition represents a significant step forward for us, expanding our presence across the viral and non-viral cell therapy development and manufacturing workflow, while projecting to nearly double our revenue base and accelerate our path to profitability. From day one, Akron provides us with an established portfolio of clinical and commercial programs supported by Akron’s DMFs and reagents. By bringing together two highly complementary businesses, we are diversifying our revenue base, increasing our mix of recurring revenue and expanding our exposure to the growth of commercially approved cell therapies, positioning MaxCyte for more durable near- and long-term growth. Like MaxCyte, Akron has become a trusted supplier to leading biopharma companies by delivering differentiated, high-quality products and best-in-class service. Akron is a market leader in the mission-critical consumables required for cell therapy manufacturing, including cytokines, growth factors, human plasma-derived products and media. We are excited to work alongside the talented Akron team as we bring together two companies to deepen customer relationships and better support cell therapy developers from development through commercialization.”
Maher Masoud, President and CEO of MaxCyte
“We are tremendously excited by the opportunity to join these two world-class organizations, leveraging our collective experience and expertise to support our partners as they bring transformative therapies to patients around the world. At Akron, we have always believed in earning our partners’ trust through consistent execution, uncompromising quality, and a deep commitment to the patients they serve. As part of MaxCyte, we remain committed to delivering the quality, reliability, and innovation our partners have come to expect.”
Ezequiel Zylberberg, COO of Akron Bio
“Akron Bio’s success reflects the dedication of its team, and we believe MaxCyte is the best partner to drive continued growth and expand its impact on patients. Our decision to accept MaxCyte shares as part of the consideration reflects our confidence in the combined company’s long-term value and allows us to participate in its future success.”
Arcline Investment Management

candidates.title: Addex Spin-out Neurosterix Closes $105 Million Series B Financing
candidates.snippet: Addex Spin-out Neurosterix Closes $105 Million Series B Financing GlobeNewswire
candidates.text:
Ad Hoc Announcement Pursuant to Art. 53 LR
Geneva, Switzerland, November 11, 2026 - Addex Therapeutics (SIX and Nasdaq: ADXN), a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company focused on developing a portfolio of novel small molecule allosteric modulators for neurological disorders, today announced that its spin-out company, Neurosterix, has closed a $105 million Series B financing from a syndicate of leading life science investors. Addex did not participate in the financing and its equity interest now represents 8.5% of the issued capital at a valuation of $18.6 million.
The proceeds raised will support mainly the planned Phase 2 clinical development of NTX-253, a highly selective muscarinic M4 positive allosteric modulator (PAM), for schizophrenia. The financing will also support Neurosterix’s broader pipeline of selective allosteric modulators for a range of neuropsychiatric disorders.
“The closing of this significant financing is a huge endorsement of the allosteric approach pioneered by Addex in schizophrenia as well as other neuropsychiatric disorders. Congatulations to the whole Neurosterix team, which has made enormous strides in advancing lead program NTX-253 through clinical development and ready for Phase 2, following our spin-out in 2024,” said Tim Dyer, CEO of Addex.
About NTX-253 and M4 PAMs
The M4 muscarinic receptor is a validated target for treating schizophrenia and related disorders through indirect modulation of dopamine signaling. NTX-253 is a potent, highly selective, oral PAM of M4 that fine-tunes muscarinic signaling in the brain to potentially reduce psychosis symptoms while avoiding the movement disorders and metabolic complications associated with traditional dopamine antagonists. Neurosterix has completed Phase 1 single- and multiple-ascending-dose clinical studies of NTX-253, which data supporting advancing into larger scale Phase 2 clinical studies.
About Neurosterix
Neurosterix is a clinical-stage biotechnology company focused on transforming neuropsychiatric care through selective allosteric modulation. The company’s approach is designed to fine-tune brain signaling with greater precision and selectivity, with the goal of developing safer, more effective treatments for people living with schizophrenia, and mood and anxiety disorders. Neurosterix’s pipeline includes NTX-253, a selective muscarinic M4 positive allosteric modulator (PAM) for schizophrenia; NTX-819, a potentially first-in-class mGlu7 negative allosteric modulator (NAM) for mood and anxiety disorders; and NTX-529, a second differentiated M4 PAM for additional psychosis- and mood-related disorders. Neurosterix has operations in Boston and Geneva. For more information, visit www.neurosterix.com.
About Addex Therapeutics
Addex Therapeutics is a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company focused on developing a portfolio of novel small molecule allosteric modulators for neurological disorders. Addex's lead drug candidate, dipraglurant (mGlu5 negative allosteric modulator or NAM), is under evaluation for future development in brain injury recovery, including post-stroke and traumatic brain injury recovery. Addex has selected a GABAB PAM drug candidate for development in substance use disorders and has successfully completed IND enabling studies. In addition, Addex is advancing a differentiated GABAB PAM compound for the treatment of chronic cough. Addex holds a 8.5% equity interest in a private spin out company, Neurosterix US Holdings LLC, which is advancing a portfolio of allosteric modulator programs, including M4 PAM for schizophrenia, psychosis and mood-related disorders and mGlu7 NAM for mood disorders. Addex has also invested in Stalicla, a private Swiss company pioneering a precision medicine approach for neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders.
Addex shares are listed on the SIX Swiss Exchange and American Depositary Shares representing its shares are listed on the NASDAQ Capital Market, and trade under the ticker symbol “ADXN” on each exchange. For more information, visit www.addextherapeutics.com .

Clara Raises $105 Million to Grow Latin American Corporate Spend Management Platform
By Julie Muhn (@julieschicktanz) Posted on November 13, 2026
Categories: Daily news , Funding
Clara raised $105 million, comprising a $65 million Series C equity round and the renewal of a $40 million growth financing facility, bringing its total debt and equity funding to $838 million.
Clara will use the funding to expand its market reach and enhance its AI capabilities, including its MCP integration that enables AI agents to access financial data and execute authorized transactions.
The funding comes amid global growth in corporate card and spend management platforms, as providers expand beyond payments and expense tracking to offer integrated, AI-powered financial management tools.
Brazil-based spend management platform Clara raised $105 million this week. The round is comprised of $65 million in equity in a Series C round and the renewal of a $40 million growth financing facility from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund (CVF).
The $65 million Series C was anchored by Citius, Kaszek, and DEG, a subsidiary of Germany’s KfW Group. The round also attracted participation from 10 existing investors and three new investors, including CMT Digital and Nascent VC.
The latest investment brings Clara’s total debt and equity funding to $838 million, following several debt financing deals over the past year. In November 2025, Clara secured $70 million in structured debt financing from BBVA Spark, Covalto, and the International Finance Corporation (IFC). Three months later, the company renewed a $150 million credit facility with Goldman Sachs, bringing its total debt capacity to more than $250 million.
Clara will use today’s funding to expand its go-to-market team and strengthen the automation and AI capabilities of its platform. Clara was founded in 2020 and now helps more than 45,000 businesses automate routine work, control spending, and make better financial decisions. The company’s platform offers corporate cards, bill payments, spend management, accounts payable, and accounts receivable to help businesses make and manage payments. Along with the financing announcement, Clara said it has also surpassed $100 million in annualized net revenue and maintained positive EBITDA for more than a year.
Among Clara’s capabilities is its Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration, which connects the platform with AI agents to enable customers to access real-time spending reports and forecasts using natural language, as well as execute authorized transactions autonomously. The company also offers AI-powered policy enforcement that checks employee expenses against company policies in real time, global spend management tools that allow businesses to manage expenses across countries and currencies, and fleet management solutions that support fuel payments and vehicle operations.
“Clara exists to champion Latin American businesses, and we work tirelessly to give them the tools to compete and win on the global stage,” said Clara Co-Founder and CEO Gerry Giacomán Colyer. “The region has long been underserved by financial platforms designed for other markets. We’re combining AI with local expertise to solve challenges specific to doing business here and give our customers a distinct competitive edge.”
Clara’s latest funding comes as spend management platforms increasingly look beyond corporate cards and expense tracking. By combining payments, financial data, and AI-driven automation, Clara is positioning itself to help businesses manage not just how they spend money, but how they make financial decisions.
The news of Clara’s growth comes as corporate card and spend management fintechs around the world are expanding their customer bases as well as their offerings. Companies such as Ramp and Brex in the US, Pleo and Payhawk in Europe, and Airwallex in Asia-Pacific have expanded beyond corporate cards to offer more comprehensive financial management platforms. These providers have integrated payments, expense management, accounts payable, and AI-powered automation into a single offering. Clara is following a similar trajectory in Latin America, where its regional focus and growing suite of financial tools position it to compete for businesses looking to consolidate and automate their financial operations.

SALT LAKE CITY , Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Databento, the market data platform for modern finance, today announced a $100 million Series C financing at a $1.1 billion valuation. The round was led by Fifth Down Capital, an early investor in Databento, with participation from nearly all of the company's existing investors, including NEA, DRW Venture Capital, Tribe Capital, and Hedosophia.
The announcement follows Databento's $97 million Series B earlier this year. Since closing its previous round, the company has more than doubled its revenue while remaining profitable.
Databento serves leading quantitative trading firms, brokerages, asset managers, commodities firms, and digital asset companies. The company has also established a strong presence in artificial intelligence, having signed enterprise contracts with five of the six leading frontier AI labs.
Databento had 39 employees when it closed its Series C, reaching a $1.1 billion valuation with a fraction of the headcount of traditional market data providers.
"In this AI era, we're seeing remarkably small teams build billion-dollar companies, but that level of efficiency is unprecedented in the market data industry," said Christina Qi, co-founder and CEO of Databento. "Until now, reaching this milestone required hundreds of employees given the sheer scale of physical infrastructure involved. I'm incredibly proud of what we've accomplished, and we'll continue to prioritize exceptional talent as we grow."
"Fifth Down first invested in Databento pre-revenue, as we recognized early on that the company had an opportunity to challenge the established model for delivering financial market data," said Andrew Spellman, founder and CEO of Fifth Down Capital. "Our confidence has only grown as Databento's traction and execution have demonstrated it can serve demanding institutional customers, sustain rapid growth, and build a profitable business. Databento's performance has reinforced our original thesis and strengthened our conviction in the company. We are thankful to Christina and Luca for the opportunity to increase our investment and involvement by leading the Series C financing."
The round also included a strategic investment from Fitch Ventures, bringing the perspective of a leading financial information provider with deep expertise in credit ratings, financial data, and market insights.
"Financial data is becoming increasingly API-driven and machine-consumed, creating an opportunity to fundamentally rethink how institutions and other market participants access it," said Gabby Munoz, Global Head of M&A and Venture Investments at Fitch Group. "Databento has built differentiated infrastructure at the source and paired it with a modern, self-service model that makes institutional-grade market data available on demand. We're excited to back the team as they scale a platform we believe will help shape how market data is captured, delivered, and consumed."
The new funding will support Databento's continued investment in its market data infrastructure and expansion into additional asset classes.
About Databento
Databento is the market data platform for modern finance. The company provides real-time and historical data across futures, options, equities, and indices through a unified API. By owning the entire stack from source to delivery, Databento is the first platform of its kind to combine the performance and reliability demanded by the world's leading trading firms with a dramatically simpler developer experience. To learn more about Databento, visit databento.com .
About Fifth Down Capital
Founded in 2014, Fifth Down Capital is a network-based investment firm that invests in private companies and funds. Fifth Down currently manages over 70 investment vehicles and has a full-time team of 30 professionals. For more information, visit fifthdown.com .

Israeli-American cybersecurity startup Daylight has raised $80 million in a Series B funding round that brings the total raised by the company to $120 million.
The investment round was led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives’ Growth Equity, with additional support from Okta Ventures, Bain Capital, Craft Ventures, Vintage Partners, and Maple Capital.

Venture capital investor Course Corrected announced today that it has raised €80 million (USD$89 million) at the final close of its second fund, focused on investing in early-stage European technology companies across the energy and resource transition.
Founded in 2021 by Christine Ahlstrand, Kerstin Cooley and Katja Bergman, Stockholm-based Course Corrected invests in early-stage technology companies developing solutions to enable industries to become more energy, resource and cost efficient. Fund II builds on the firm’s first fund, which focused entirely on climate tech.
According to the firm, Fund II will invest in 20 – 30 companies across key themes including energy systems, industrial optimization and automation, electrification and resource-smart solutions, focusing on scalable businesses whose products advance the energy and resource transition.

“We invest to generate strong financial returns. Impact is how we get there: by backing juggernauts that solve real problems, scale commercially, and transform industries for the better.”
Fund II invests only in European companies. Christine Ahlstrand, founding partner at Course Corrected, said:
“Europe has the research, the technology, the founders and the markets. But who will own the next generation of industry if we do not finance the companies building it?”
To date, Fund II has made seven investments, including Tavion, Renasens, eComID and Skye.

By Amit Chowdhry

Eli Radiopharma: Nearly $60 Million Series A Financing To Advance Radiopharmaceutical Pipeline Toward Clinical Development
Eli Radiopharma has raised nearly $60 million (RMB 400 million) in Series A financing to advance its radiopharmaceutical pipeline toward clinical development. The funding will support preclinical research, regulatory submissions, early-stage clinical studies, and the expansion of the company’s research and development capabilities.
Huagai Capital led the financing round, with Bayland Capital serving as co-lead investor. Additional participants included Boyu Ventures, Delian Capital, InnoPinnacle Fund, Haibang Venture, Bairui Capital, Shenzhen Angel FOF Management, and Grand Flight Investment.
Existing shareholders CSPC & Growth Bio Fund, Huaige Capital, KHK Fund, Longfeng Venture, Hongsheng Capital, Bioclub Fund, and Skyfield Capital also participated in the financing.
Eli Radiopharma plans to allocate the proceeds toward preclinical research, investigational new drug applications, and early-stage clinical development. The company will also strengthen its research platforms, recruit additional talent, expand clinical operations, and pursue business development opportunities.
Founded in 2024, Eli Radiopharma focuses on developing radiopharmaceutical products that combine molecular targeting with radionuclide technology. Its pipeline includes diagnostic and therapeutic candidates designed to address unmet medical needs in oncology and neurological diseases.
The company has advanced multiple programs targeting novel molecular mechanisms through lead discovery, laboratory validation, and animal studies. Several candidates are approaching investigational new drug submissions, representing an important transition from early research toward human clinical testing.
Radiopharmaceuticals combine targeting molecules with radioactive isotopes to identify or treat diseased tissue. Therapeutic radioligands are designed to deliver radiation directly to tumors while limiting exposure to surrounding healthy tissue. Related diagnostic imaging agents can help physicians identify appropriate patients, evaluate disease progression, and monitor treatment responses.
The financing also reflects growing international interest in radiopharmaceutical innovation originating in China. Global pharmaceutical companies have increasingly explored opportunities involving novel molecular targets, therapeutic radionuclides, and expanded clinical applications.
Eli Radiopharma’s investors identified these areas as important drivers of future industry growth, particularly as radiopharmaceutical technologies move into additional cancer indications and other therapeutic applications.
The company’s longer-term strategy includes building a globally competitive pipeline capable of serving patients in international markets, including the U.S. and Europe. Its immediate priorities involve completing preclinical development, meeting regulatory requirements, and advancing differentiated candidates into clinical studies.
The Series A financing provides Eli Radiopharma with additional resources to move its lead programs closer to clinical validation while expanding the infrastructure needed to support a broader radiopharmaceutical development portfolio.

Dr. Feng Yu, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Eli Radiopharma

Every time a company lets an AI agent access data, update a customer record, approve a request, or change a production system, it delegates authority. The same permissions that let an agent get work done can let it expose sensitive data, make changes outside company policy, disrupt a critical workflow, or rack up huge inference costs.
"Agent builders from the AI labs, hyperscalers, and thousands of startups make it easy to deploy powerful agents across the business," said Ron Williams, founder and CEO of Kindo. "What's missing is the tooling that lets an organization centrally control how those agents are built, what data they can reach, where that data can go, and what they cost, while also allowing support teams to reach in and fix an agent at any hour. The teams that must support and control AI, IT, Security, Finance, and Compliance, get a single set of controls: what employees can do with an agent, what an agent can touch, how it behaves around the clock, and what it costs. The result is an AI Operations Center, SOC- and NOC-style monitoring and intervention for AI, where those teams eliminate risk, drive down cost, and make sure AI delivers measurable outcomes.
Implementation is turnkey and is run by the IT operations staff an organization already has. Teams connect the agents, data sources, and AI models already in use, and from that moment everything is discovered, observed, and controlled from one place. Charta Health: $55 Million Series B To Expand AI Medical Chart Review
Charta Health has raised $55 million in Series B funding to expand its artificial intelligence platform for medical chart review and create a common standard of billing accuracy for healthcare providers and insurers. Insight Partners led the round, with participation from existing investors Madrona, Bain Capital Ventures, and South Park Commons, along with QuantumLight.
Charta applies AI to unstructured clinical information, including physician notes, scanned orders, laboratory results, and images. Its technology reviews medical records to determine whether documented care supports the codes used for billing.
The company wants providers and payers to resolve coding discrepancies before a claim is submitted rather than through denials, audits, and appeals. Those administrative processes contribute billions of dollars in costs to the U.S. healthcare system.
Charta for Providers reviews every chart before billing and checks the documentation against official coding guidance, payer rules, and an organization’s clinical protocols. Findings are presented within electronic health record workflows for human approval.

Its six products cover retrospective hierarchical condition category coding, automated second-pass reviews, coder workflows, prospective risk-adjustment intelligence, audit preparation, and quality care-gap detection.

Bay, an AI security platform for agentic enterprises, has emerged from stealth with $50 million in total funding, including a $37 million Series A led by Battery Ventures and a $13 million seed led by YL Ventures and Striker Venture Partners.
The Tel Aviv-based company evaluates each AI agent action in the context of the full session and decides in milliseconds whether it can proceed, deploying across devices, cloud and SaaS in under five minutes without extra endpoint agents or network proxies.

PRESS RELEASE —  Bay , the AI security platform building the trust layer for agentic enterprises, has emerged from stealth less than a year after its founding with dozens of enterprise customers, including Micron, Peloton, ClickUp and Wix. Bay addresses a primary barrier to AI adoption by allowing autonomous agents to perform business-critical work safely while enterprises retain control and accountability at scale.
Bay has raised $50 million in total funding. We believe that this trust layer will become essential infrastructure for the agentic era.”
Bay grew out of the same problem it now solves for customers. Its founders watched one of their coding agents try to expose a cloud environment to the internet to complete a test. The agent had not been compromised. It used legitimate permissions to pursue a legitimate goal in a dangerous way.
Bay brings AI governance and enforcement across employee devices, cloud infrastructure, and SaaS applications in under 5 minutes, without an additional persistent endpoint agent, kernel driver, or network proxy. It secures the full range of AI that enterprises are deploying through a single platform that covers multiple use cases under one set of policies. Bay combines AI discovery and posture management, session-level observability, and real-time enforcement, and connects to existing security workflows for automated remediation.
“In Bay, we saw a company we felt had a differentiated technical approach that was already winning enterprise customers at an early stage,” said Dharmesh Thakker, General Partner at Battery Ventures. “That combination gave us conviction to lead the round. We believe Bay can become a core control layer for companies putting AI agents to work at scale.”
“We evaluated a crowded field of companies addressing AI agent security, and Bay stood out because it can understand and control individual agent actions, from the endpoint to the cloud, while fitting into infrastructure enterprises already use,” said Yoav Leitersdorf, managing partner at YL Ventures. “We believe Bay can become as fundamental to enterprise AI adoption as the network firewall was to the internet era.”
Bay evaluates each proposed action in the context of the full agent session and decides locally in milliseconds whether it can proceed. Instead of requiring security teams to write and maintain rules for every new agent or tool, Bay learns from the organization’s agent activity and interprets context around each action in real time, distinguishing between activity that looks identical in isolation but carries very different risks. As teams add new agents and workflows, Bay adapts its policies and expands the work agents can safely do on their own. The platform works across the AI models, assistants, and agent frameworks an organization chooses.
“If you’re a security leader at an enterprise today, you’re likely facing one of two realities: either AI agents have already spread across your organization and it’s the Wild West, or your leadership has mandated an enterprise-wide AI rollout by the end of the year to accelerate the business,” said Yuval Zacharia, co-founder and CEO of Bay. “Either way, the challenge is the same: enabling AI adoption at scale without losing control. Bay was built to be the one platform that secures every way the enterprise uses AI, so security becomes the reason AI ships faster, not the reason it stalls.”
Zacharia founded Bay alongside CPO Aner Morag and VP of R&D Boris Danilovich. Zacharia began her career in Israeli intelligence at Unit 8200, where she led a department of 50 people before becoming the first-ever intelligence officer to transition into offensive cybersecurity and was assigned to the unit’s most elite department. Alta has raised $47.5 million in a Series A round to build a compliance-focused blockchain for banks and large companies. Index Ventures led the round, which Alta announced Tuesday, according to Fortune’s report .
The company is developing its own blockchain with a compliance layer that lets customers ensure processed transactions follow rules and regulations around the world. Alta is pitching the system to financial firms and large companies seeking faster money transfers with crypto.
Why Alta Is Building a Compliance-Focused Blockchain
Financial firms already have a choice of networks, including Ethereum, Solana and Avalanche. Alta chief executive Loong Wang told Fortune he believes blockchain is the best technology for transferring money, but said existing options lack privacy and compliance tools designed for banks and other large financial players. Glass office tower viewed from below beneath clouds.
Wang said Alta’s features include a tool that prevents people from sending funds at random to addresses on its blockchain. The feature addresses a practice known as an airdrop, which can require wallet holders to accept funds whether they want them or not.
“We often say we wouldn’t have built an L-1 if we didn’t have to,” Wang told Fortune. His comments describe the company’s rationale for creating another network despite the many Layer 1 blockchains already available.
Airwallex Provides a Distribution Connection
Alta previously raised $32.5 million in seed funding, backed primarily by Airwallex, the Australian fintech company competing with Stripe and others in global payments. Alta has 25 employees and offices in San Francisco and Melbourne.
Fortune reported that Wang has a personal connection with Airwallex chief executive Jack Zhang. Zhang had been skeptical of crypto, but recently acknowledged the inherent value of stablecoins for cheap and efficient money transfers.
Airwallex is also serving as a distribution channel, encouraging its global customer network to use Alta’s platform for crypto transactions. The relationship comes as Airwallex rivals build crypto infrastructure too, including Stripe and its Tempo blockchain.
“With the rise of agentic banking and programmable payments, stablecoins are becoming an important vector for settlement,” Zhang said in a statement announcing Alta’s funding round.
Investors Join Alta’s Series A
GV (Google Ventures), Blackbird Ventures, Square Peg and Capital49 also participated in the Series A. Capital49 is a venture firm established by Airwallex’s cofounders. The company did not disclose its valuation in the round.
Alta was previously known as Metal and recently rebranded. Wang founded an earlier crypto startup that he sold in 2021, then pivoted to a second startup using quantum computing to aid drug discovery before returning to crypto technology to found Alta with Catherine Porter, a former Meta executive.
The round places Alta among companies building transaction infrastructure for institutional crypto use. Banks are also exploring stablecoin settlement and digital asset infrastructure, including efforts discussed at MERGE Madrid 2026 . Other coverage has examined how banks put deposits on blockchain and plans for a shared banking network . Those initiatives provide context for the institutional market Alta is pursuing, while the company’s stated next step is to attract banks and large companies to its own network.

Alta announced a $47.5 million Series A round led by Index Ventures.
What is Alta building?
Alta is building its own blockchain with a compliance layer intended for banks and large companies. The company says its tools address privacy and compliance needs.
What does Alta's compliance layer do?
The layer lets customers ensure transactions they process are consistent with rules and regulations around the world, according to the source.
How is Airwallex connected to Alta?
Airwallex primarily backed Alta’s $32.5 million seed round and is encouraging customers in its global network to use Alta’s platform for crypto transactions.

San Francisco startup Mount Thor has raised $45 million in seed and Series A equity funding to expand cloud infrastructure that gives AI developers on-demand access to Apple’s macOS operating system and silicon.
According to the company , CRV and Conviction co-led the Series A, while Chad Byers and Offline Ventures co-led the seed round. Founded in 2026, Mount Thor develops and operates data center systems built around Apple hardware, providing computing resources for AI research, software development and running AI models.
The financing will support additional computing capacity and hiring, particularly as the company develops infrastructure for running open-source AI models on Apple silicon.
Building Infrastructure for AI Agents
Mount Thor is focused on developers of AI agents that use computers to perform tasks, including those requiring software available only on macOS, by building and managing rack-scale systems of Apple hardware to allow customers to access computing environments remotely rather than maintain their own equipment.
“Making Apple’s operating system and silicon available at datacenter-scale is a massive untapped opportunity in AI infrastructure,” said Peter Voell, Founder and CEO of Mount Thor. “Decades of investment in accessibility and human-computer interaction make macOS the best place for agents to work and for humans to hold them accountable. And with chips like the M5 Ultra, Apple silicon is becoming a high performance, more power- and cost- efficient platform for production inference.”
Mount Thor identified several uses for the infrastructure:
AI research: Creating reinforcement learning environments for computer-use models.
Agent testing: Providing secure macOS environments for developing and evaluating AI agents.
Long-running operations: Supporting agents that operate for weeks across a user’s devices using the same Apple identity.
Software development: Building, testing and simulating applications for Apple devices.
AI inference: Running open-source models optimized for Apple silicon.
Mount Thor reported deploying its first data center in less than six months and plans to increase capacity as demand grows. Its team includes people who previously developed infrastructure at Cerebras, CoreWeave, Fluidstack, Nebius, OpenAI and xAI.

British Business Bank: Additional £40 Million Commitment Supports Harwood Fund
The British Business Bank has committed an additional £40 million to Harwood Private Capital to increase the availability of flexible financing for smaller and lower-middle-market businesses across the United Kingdom.
The investment supports the first closing of Harwood Private Capital UK Fund II. Commitments to the fund and its related co-investment vehicles now total approximately £120 million.
Harwood will use the capital to provide debt financing for privately held companies pursuing organic expansion, acquisitions, and shareholder transitions. The strategy gives business owners an alternative to conventional bank lending or a complete sale through an M&A transaction.
The commitment increases the British Business Bank’s total investment with Harwood to £75 million. The government-owned development bank previously committed £35 million to the manager’s inaugural HPC UK SME Fund in 2020.
Harwood specializes in flexible private-credit solutions for lower-middle-market companies. Its target borrowers include founder- and family-owned businesses that need additional growth capital but want to preserve ownership and strategic control.
The inaugural fund invested across digital technology, clean-energy supply chains, manufacturing, tourism, and other sectors. One portfolio example is Western Marinas, a Welsh marina operator that used Harwood financing to restore facilities in Wales and southwest England.
That investment supported local jobs and family-operated businesses while attracting visitors and economic activity to surrounding coastal communities. It demonstrates how private credit can finance physical assets and regional companies that may not fit the standardized requirements of traditional lenders.
The British Business Bank’s mandate is to improve access to capital for smaller companies and address financing gaps that can limit growth, productivity, and job creation. In its 2025-2026 financial year, the bank supported £9.4 billion of financing for approximately 38,000 businesses.
That total included £1.3 billion of public funding, £4.3 billion of private capital attracted through the bank’s programs, and £3.7 billion of guaranteed lending. Around 30,000 recipients had not previously received support through the institution.
Harwood Private Capital UK Fund II is intended to extend this impact by supplying customized debt structures for companies whose requirements may not be served adequately by banks or private equity investors.

candidates.title: Graphon Labs Raises $35M Series A to Give AI Agents Long-Term Memory
candidates.snippet: Graphon Labs Raises $35M Series A to Give AI Agents Long-Term Memory Wowtale
candidates.text:
AI models keep getting smarter, yet they still struggle to understand the videos, documents and conversations people have accumulated. A startup building memory infrastructure that preserves the structure of that data has now raised a Series A.
Graphon Labs announced a $35 million Series A on Nov. 10. RRE Ventures led the round, and according to the press release, HP, Energy Impact Partners, Hitachi Ventures and Gaia VC participated. It comes six months after the company’s seed round and brings total funding to $43.3 million. Graphon plans to use the money to expand its infrastructure for developers and enterprise customers, then extend from the cloud and on-premises deployments to consumer devices.
The seed round drew some attention in Korea. According to May reports from The Next Web and SiliconAngle, Novera Ventures led the $8.3 million seed, with Perplexity Fund, Hitachi Ventures, Gaia Ventures, Samsung Next and GS Futures also participating. The Next Web reported that GS Group is an early customer, using the technology for convenience-store traffic analysis and safety monitoring on construction sites.
The problem Graphon targets is that AI “memory” today is mostly storage. Fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) have been used to bring company knowledge into models, but when documents are cut into pieces and searched as vectors, sentences with nearly identical words and opposite meanings, such as “refund allowed” and “refund not allowed,” can land close together. A rule may be found while the fragment holding its exception is missed. The company likens it to tearing a book apart page by page, crumpling the pages and trying to find them again.
Its answer is to keep the structure. Graphon reads mixed data such as video, images, spreadsheets, recordings and markdown files and builds a detailed graph without deciding in advance which relationships will matter. It then uses a compressed representation of that graph, the “graphon,” to guide where to search. According to press reports, the graphon is a mathematical concept formalized around 2008 by UC Berkeley professors Jennifer Chayes and Christian Borgs, among others, and the two serve as technical advisers.
Developers use it much like S3: put files in a bucket and Graphon builds the structure. The website lists four APIs, Storage, Search, Answer and Research. Products are split into Graphon Enterprise, Graphon Developer and Graphon On-Device Memory for phones, laptops, cameras and wearables, and enterprise customers can choose hosted, customer-managed VPC or on-premises deployment.
The performance figures are the company’s own. Graphon says it scored 93.9% accuracy on the LoCoMo conversational memory benchmark while using 58% fewer tokens than loading the full conversation, and 90.2% accuracy with 95% token savings on ConvoMem. On ATM-Bench, which spans video, audio and text, it reported 81.7%, 5.0 percentage points ahead of the next entry on the public leaderboard. None of these numbers has been independently verified.
Disclosed customers include the San Francisco 49ers and Hitachi Rail. The 49ers are weighing it for finding sponsorship opportunities and supporting staff work, while Hitachi Rail is evaluating its potential to surface contextual knowledge in industrial settings and improve AI reasoning. RRE Ventures’ Raju Rishi pointed to the fact that models can reason and agents can act, yet neither improves without accumulating knowledge, as the reason for investing.
The company is led by CEO Arbaaz Khan , who said in the company blog that working as an applied scientist on an Amazon customer service team made him feel the gap between a plausible answer and a correct one. He founded the company with Clark, with whom he had researched graph-based techniques since their PhD days to help robots remember where they had been and explore unfamiliar environments. May reports named Clark Zhang as chief technology officer and Deepak Mishra as chief operating officer. The company says its team includes engineers and researchers from Amazon, Meta, Google, Apple and NVIDIA.
Several startups are already competing in the agent memory layer. Mem0 lets developers add persistent memory to AI with a few lines of code and has raised $24 million across its seed and Series A. Supermemory , founded by a 19-year-old, raised a $3 million seed for a memory engine that analyzes documents, chats and emails. Memories.ai focuses on video memory, processing up to 10 million hours of footage, and raised an $8 million seed with Samsung Next participating. Letta , backed by Felicis, is also named as a rival. While those companies lean toward particular kinds of data such as conversation logs or video, Graphon pitches weaving video, documents and spreadsheets into a single graph.

Orakl Oncology Raises $34M Series A to Expand AI Cancer Drug Prediction

Norrsken VC announced on November 12, 2026 that it co-led Orakl Oncology’s oversubscribed $34 million Series A alongside Singular, bringing the AI drug-development company’s total funding to $50 million.
Orakl plans to expand its dataset and AI research team, increase data generation fivefold and move beyond colorectal and pancreatic cancers into lung and gastric cancers. The proceeds are also intended to establish US and UK teams, deploy predictions across more than 10 drug programs and discover and validate drug co-targets from patient biology and experimental screens.
New investors InfraVia, Serena, the Patient Autonome Fund managed by Bpifrance, teampact.ventures and Plug and Play joined the round, alongside existing backers Verve Ventures, Speedinvest and HCVC.
Patient-Derived Data and AI
Founded in 2023 as a spin-out of Gustave Roussy, Orakl grows patient-derived tumor organoids, which are laboratory models of individual patients’ cancers, and screens them against drugs. Its platform overview describes results enriched with genomic, transcriptomic and phenotypic data and anchored to longitudinal clinical histories, creating a multimodal dataset for its predictive systems.
Orakl’s biopharma products are divided between O-Predict and O-Target. O-Predict is designed to anticipate trial endpoints including tumor response, progression-free survival and overall survival, identify biomarkers that distinguish likely responders, assess drug combinations and compare benefit-risk profiles. O-Target focuses on therapeutic-target discovery.
Norrsken calls the resulting patient cohorts virtual cancer patients . The drug-response measurements must be generated through patient samples, laboratory infrastructure and hospital partnerships rather than assembled from existing databases. Every experiment adds proprietary data connecting patient biology, clinical information and observed drug responses.
What the SCOPE Preprint Shows
Orakl reports 90% accuracy for prospective predictions of individual patient responses across more than 30 clinical trials. A separate April 2026 preprint co-authored by Orakl staff provides detailed arm-level results for SCOPE, the Screening-to-Clinical Outcome Prediction Engine. It is marked as early-stage research that may not yet have been peer reviewed.
SCOPE was trained on 54 treatment lines from 52 patients with metastatic colorectal or pancreatic cancer, using matched clinical data and organoid screens covering nine compounds. To predict trial outcomes, it generated synthetic patient profiles from published eligibility criteria and matched them to a biobank of 81 patient-derived organoid lines.
External validation covered 32 arms from 23 published trials. The authors report an R² of 0.85 and a mean absolute error of 0.82 months for predicted median progression-free survival, the time patients live without disease progression. For objective response rate—the share of patients with a measured tumor response—R² was 0.71 and mean absolute error was 7.3 percentage points. Combining organoid and clinical data significantly outperformed either data type alone.
SCOPE also selected the superior treatment arm in seven of eight head-to-head comparisons. The preprint describes a prospective application to daraxonrasib before Phase III data became available, in which the platform predicted superiority over standard chemotherapy in KRAS-mutant metastatic pancreatic cancer.
Commercial Pipeline and Expansion
Just over a year after commercial launch, Norrsken reports that 18 of the world’s 20 largest pharmaceutical companies are in Orakl’s commercial pipeline. The figure covers pipeline participation rather than signed customers; the first pharmaceutical engagements have become multi-year collaborations. More than 15 additional cancer centers across Europe, North America and Asia are in contract negotiations.
Orakl has more than 40 employees, 30% of whom hold PhDs. Its co-founders are CEO Fanny Jaulin, CTO Gustave Ronteix and COO Diane-Laure Pagès, whose backgrounds span cancer biology, AI, data science, oncology and hospital partnerships.
The next phase will test whether Orakl can extend that patient-derived data model into additional cancers while converting its broad pharmaceutical pipeline into more multi-year drug-development collaborations.

candidates.title: Exclusive: SE3, a German startup building ‘spatial intelligence’ for military drones, gets $30 million in Series A funding
candidates.snippet: Exclusive: SE3, a German startup building ‘spatial intelligence’ for military drones, gets $30 million in Series A funding Fortune
candidates.text:
SE3, a Munich-based startup that makes AI software to help drones and other unmanned military systems understand the three-dimensional world around them, has raised $30 million in a Series A round led by Accel.
Recommended Video
Keen, Lakestar, and Seedcamp also participated in the funding round. It comes less than five months after the company, which recently dropped “Labs” from its name, emerged from stealth with €5.5 million ($6.1 million) in seed funding.
SE3’s software takes video and sensor feeds from multiple drones and ground vehicles and fuses them into a single 3D picture of the battlefield—”like a mini map, how you would know it from a strategy game,” cofounder and CEO Lukas Köstler told Fortune .
On top of that map sits a layer that labels objects and how they relate to one another, so soldiers can query it in plain language: How do I reach a target without being seen? What’s a good route for a heavy vehicle?
Operators can also give commands the same way. Rather than remotely piloting a drone with a joystick or having to tap away on a tablet, a soldier can simply say, “I need reconnaissance two kilometers in the north over the forest,” Köstler said, and a suitable drone would take off, fly the mission, and report back.
In addition to this map-level understanding of the battlefield, SE3 also builds the AI systems that sit inside the drones or other unmanned systems, giving them the ability to maneuver and navigate, even in cases where GPS is jammed, detect objects, and act as a “swarm” with other drones.
Köstler, who previously worked on Tesla’s Autopilot team and at Nvidia Research, said the most basic capability—drones locating themselves without GPS—has been delivered thousands of times and is “very robust.”
But he said the high-level fleet command AI is less mature. SE3 has contracts with Germany’s armed forces, the Bundeswehr, to develop it and has demonstrated it with them, but “there’s still much that needs to be built out over the next one or two years,” he said. The company also has contracts in Ukraine, where its technology is already deployed.
SE3 does not rely on general-purpose, large language models to understand physics or terrain. Instead, it uses classical computer vision algorithms to distill vast amounts of sensor data into a database a language model can query, and gives the model a harness equipped with a variety of conventional software tools the model can call. If the model needs a flight path, a conventional planning algorithm calculates one—avoiding mountains or enemy lines of sight, for example.
Simply feeding raw data to the model “wouldn’t work at all,” Köstler said. Actions such as a drone takeoff can be set to require a human operator’s approval. The system can run entirely offline, and customers can swap in their own preferred frontier AI model to act as the “brains” of the system.
SE3 spun out of the computer vision lab of Daniel Cremers at the Technical University of Munich (TUM), where Köstler and SE3’s CTO, Simon Klenk, were PhD students. Cremers serves as SE3’s chief science officer.
Military work has long made some AI researchers uneasy—a tension highlighted when the Pentagon designated Anthropic a supply-chain risk in March after it refused to let its models be used for fully autonomous weapons or mass domestic surveillance.
As a German company, SE3 is bound by strict export laws, Köstler noted: “It’s really the elected parliament that decides in the end what we will do.” SE3 serves European NATO members and their allies.
SE3 is betting that militaries will want AI software that isn’t tied to any single hardware maker. If drone makers each control their own software stack, Köstler argued, customers struggle to get systems from different vendors to work together and, within two or three years, face costly lock-in.
SE3 counts sensor maker Hensoldt, drone software company Auterion, and drone developer ERC among its partners.
Accel partner Matt Robinson said SE3’s team was “uniquely qualified to take on the challenge of building spatial AI for autonomous systems—something defense primes have found so difficult to do.”
SE3 plans to use the money to grow from roughly 40 employees to about 120 and open offices in London, Berlin, the Nordics and Baltics, and Poland. Defense will drive revenue for at least the next 12 months, Köstler said, but a small team will begin exploring civilian robotics.

Nanopath Raises $25 Million to Advance Point-of-Care Vaginitis Test
Nov 12, 2026 | Womens Health |
The Series B funding will support an FDA 510(k) study and manufacturing scale-up for the company’s plasmonic biosensing assay.
Nanopath, a point-of-care diagnostics company , closed a $25 million Series B financing round, which includes $2 million in non-dilutive grant financing.
Norwest and SV Health Investors’ MedTech Convergence Fund co-led the round, with strategic participation from the Labcorp Venture Fund . New and existing investors also took part, including Elderberry Ventures, GingerBread Capital, and Alumni Ventures.
As part of the financing, Catherine Kiani, JD, managing partner at Elderberry Ventures, and Mindy Nye, PhD, vice president of Labcorp Diagnostics, joined the Nanopath board as observers.
“Nanopath is developing truly transformative technology with the potential to reshape the molecular diagnostics industry ,” says Jeff Crowe, senior managing partner at Norwest, in a release.
Funding Targets Launch Milestones
The company will use the funding to support milestones toward the potential commercial launch of its 15-minute point-of-care vaginitis assay , including manufacturing scale-up and initiation of its FDA 510(k) clinical study. Nanopath also plans to expand its team across clinical and commercial functions as it prepares for launch.
The study is also intended to support potential expansion of the company’s pipeline into urinary tract infections and sexually transmitted infections .
“This funding brings us closer to the next and most important step,” says Alison Burklund, PhD, co-founder and co-CEO of Nanopath, in a release. She described that step as translating the company’s innovation into clinical impact.
Amogha Tadimety, PhD, co-founder and co-CEO, says in a release that the company is “excited to build on this momentum as we enter our next phase of growth.”
Plasmonic Biosensing Without Amplification
Nanopath says it has developed the first clinical diagnostics platform built on plasmonic biosensing. The company’s proprietary optical biosensing technology is designed to enable molecular detection without nucleic acid amplification, a step required by PCR-based tests .
By delivering accurate results during a single visit, Nanopath aims to establish a new standard of care for women’s health and expand access to diagnostics for women across the US. Over time, the company expects the platform to expand to other clinical indications.
The vaginitis test is under development and has not been cleared or approved by the FDA. Commercial availability is subject to successful completion of development activities and applicable regulatory review.

WhiteMatter: $20 Million Series A To Expand Enterprise AI Agent Governance
By Amit Chowdhry
Nov 11, 2026
WhiteMatter: $20 Million Series A To Expand Enterprise AI Agent Governance
WhiteMatter has raised $20 million in Series A funding to expand its enterprise platform for governing autonomous artificial intelligence agents, models, tools, and interactions. Blumberg Capital led the round, with participation from existing investors Crew Capital and Sprout & Oak. WhiteMatter previously operated under the name QuilrAI.
The company developed its platform to address security and operational risks created by AI agents that can access sensitive information, generate content, make decisions, interact with software, and create or influence other agents.
WhiteMatter governs AI across endpoints, browsers, software-as-a-service applications, cloud systems, and code. It assesses agents before deployment, applies policies to their actions, monitors outcomes, and manages traffic and spending through a controlled gateway.
Its architecture can deploy a dedicated Guardian agent for every AI agent operating within a customer’s environment. When autonomous systems create additional agents, WhiteMatter can provision corresponding Guardians to extend policy enforcement.
WhiteMatter has more than 2.25 million agents under management and expects that number to exceed 5.5 million by the end of 2026. Its platform has governed 116 billion AI interactions and helped customers avoid more than 11 trillion tokens during the past nine months.
The company tripled its customer base during 2026 and increased revenue fivefold over six months. It reported approximately 200% net revenue retention with no customer churn.
Customers include Sentara Health, Alter Domus, New American Funding, Concentrix, and other large enterprises. WhiteMatter’s policy architecture delivers decisions in 2.24 milliseconds and can process as many as 7,800 actions per minute.
The new capital will support research, product development, go-to-market expansion, and additions to WhiteMatter’s executive team. The company is positioning its technology as an operational and security layer for businesses deploying AI at scale.
KEY QUOTES:
“Despite all the discussion about pausing AI development, enterprises are doing the opposite. AI technology is too powerful, the opportunity is too significant, and the competitive pressure is too real to put it back in the box. Companies that slow down AI adoption risk being overtaken by competitors that move fast, stay secure, and scale AI with confidence, which is exactly why we built WhiteMatter.”
Vidit Arora, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of WhiteMatter
“WhiteMatter is helping us scale that adoption responsibly by providing greater visibility into how AI is being used, protecting sensitive information at the point of use, and guiding our workforce toward appropriate behaviors and tools in real time. We’re not governing AI to slow innovation. We’re creating the trust and guardrails that allow us to innovate responsibly, keep saying yes, and ultimately advance our mission of improving health every day.”
Zishan Siddiqui, Chief Information Security Officer at Sentara Health
“At Alter Domus, we scale practical AI with measured returns: squads of Industrialized Agents in production, and work that used to take a quarter now takes a week. That pace is only responsible if governance keeps up. With WhiteMatter in our cyber defense stack, every agent is governed before it goes live, every tool call is policy-checked at one gateway, and the telemetry shows us where AI actually creates value. Security, adoption, and enterprise value aren’t separate conversations here. They’re one lifecycle, and we can see all of it.”
Demetry Zilberg, Chief Technology Officer of Alter Domus
“Every wave of enterprise computing eventually produced its own security layer, from the network to the cloud to identity. Agents are the next wave and could soon outnumber employees inside enterprises, requiring a governance layer built natively for them. We backed WhiteMatter because its platform approach and Guardian agent model give enterprises the guardrails an autonomous workforce needs, at a scale no human security team could manage manually.”
Pramod Gosavi of Blumberg Capital

candidates.title: Dallas AI Startup 4Minds Raises $15M Series A at $500M Valuation
candidates.snippet: Dallas AI Startup 4Minds Raises $15M Series A at $500M Valuation Dallas Innovates
candidates.text:
Dallas-based AI startup 4Minds, which emerged from stealth mode in April, is already halfway to unicorn status. The company said today that it has raised a $15 million Series A round at a $500 million post-money valuation.
Investors include Dallas-based Waterwood Capital Group and Lubbock-based Isom Holdings — both led in part by Clayton Isom, whose family founded Wichita Falls-based oil and gas management company Stephens & Johnson in the 1960s — and several family offices with ties to the energy and data center industries.
The startup plans to use the money to expand its sales and marketing teams. It focuses on selling to companies in financial services, banking, insurance, biotech, pharmaceutical and other regulated industries, as well as consumer packaged goods, retail and logistics. It also will add to its product development team.
A new way to automate enterprise AI
At 4Minds, developers created software to help large companies build AI systems that understand their business. The platform automatically pulls data from more than 40 business systems, scrubs it and organizes it into a “knowledge graph” that maps how the data is related. The knowledge graph then continuously trains the AI models on business uses, ensuring information stays current. It all runs inside a company’s own system, so its sensitive data never touches a public AI model.
It’s “the easiest way for any enterprise to build end-to-end automation for AI workloads,” co-founder and CEO Ryan Trimberger told Dallas Innovates.
The 4Minds team sees enormous potential, Trimberger said. Large companies are ramping up spending on AI. Enterprise AI spending in the U.S. reached an annualized run rate of $177 billion in September 2026, up more than fivefold from $33 billion a year earlier, according to a Menlo Ventures report .
Many companies aren’t realizing the returns they’d like from those investments, though. Factors include difficulty scrubbing data for use in an automated AI system, rising costs and data security concerns, Trimberger said. Tackling all those issues at once is 4Minds’ selling point.
“When we initially started, we were focused on making smaller [large language models] really powerful, and the thesis was around cybersecurity,” Trimberger said. “That’s just native to who we are as a business. … We realized very quickly this wasn’t just cybersecurity. This was going to be every business, every domain, every vertical.”
Building in Deep Ellum
Trimberger founded 4Minds in 2024 along with Jerome Naidoo and Jason Nocco. The three founders make up the first three minds in the company’s name. The fourth represents the company’s customers, Trimberger said.
The team stayed small at the outset, focusing exclusively on product development. As recently as February, 4Minds employed just 13 people. Today, its headcount tops 60. Trimberger said he expects that number to approach 100 by early 2027.
He declined to share the startup’s revenue targets but said, “We think we can scale and be in the nine-figure range very quickly.”
The company sells 4Minds on the AWS and Microsoft marketplaces. It’s also part of AWS’ Global Startup Program and the Microsoft for Startups Pegasus Program , and will be featured at this month’s Microsoft Ignite 2026.
Access to strong research universities played a key role in choosing Dallas as the home for 4Minds’ product team, Trimberger said.
The company has recruited several people from the University of North Texas’ data science program and has formed a relationship with Dean Kinshuk, who leads UNT’s newly named Anuradha and Vikas Sinha College of Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Analytics. It maintains similar relationships with the University of Texas at Arlington for machine learning and Southern Methodist University for cybersecurity, Trimberger said.
“We’ve been really, really intentional to try to build an ecosystem for not just hiring but for long-term, private-sector research,” he said. “We consider ourselves an AI lab, and I think a lot of that is just an extension of our higher ed partnerships.”
Its entire product team is based in North Texas, working from an office in Deep Ellum, a location that Trimberger said is a great fit.
“We needed something that was going to be modern, cool and fit what we were building,” he said. “I don’t think there’s really anybody doing this kind of frontier-level tech in DFW, so we need a space to reflect that. We are proud to be in Dallas.”
Why family offices?
Because 4Minds concentrates on the software layer of generative AI, it doesn’t need the large investments required by companies with significant infrastructure buildouts , Trimberger said. This allows what he described as an unconventional approach to fundraising, seeking smaller amounts of money from family offices.
“We’re not building infrastructure like a data center company would, so our operating capital is much lighter,” he said. “So, we’ve decided to forgo the traditional venture capital for our Series A and focus exclusively on Dallas-based family offices. That’s a strategic avenue for us.”
The startup’s investors can be a built-in customer base, as they look not just to invest in AI but to introduce AI to portfolio companies, Trimberger said. The approach also means 4Minds’ investors understand what it takes to operate and scale a business.

News provided by

SHENZHEN, China , Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Clawlab, a technology startup developing smart tools for textile creation, has raised more than $15 million in a Pre-A3 funding round led by miHoYo. Vision Plus Capital and Shunwei Capital also increased their investments through super pro rata participation. The round brings Clawlab's total funding to approximately $25 million across four equity rounds. Its shareholder base includes Sequoia China, Shunwei Capital, YM Capital, Vision Plus Capital, and miHoYo, bringing together leading venture capital firms and a strategic corporate investor.
Investors Back Clawlab's Vision for a New Consumer Category
With AI software commanding much of the market's attention, Clawlab's more than $15 million funding round reflects investor interest in a different opportunity: the untapped consumer potential of smart knitting.
The opportunity comes from a gap between rising consumer demand and the tools available to meet it. Interest in personalized, hands-on creation is growing, yet most knitting equipment remains designed for factories and professional users. Pattern development, stitch control, and machine operation still require specialist expertise. The category lacks a desktop device capable of bringing industrial-grade knitting capabilities within reach of individual creators.
Clawlab is addressing that gap with the world's first smart knitting machine designed for home use. It turns an image or idea into a finished knitted item, handling pattern preparation, stitchwork, and repetitive production while leaving the design, colors, and intended use to the user.
That flexibility supports a wide range of applications, from scarves and doll clothes to pet accessories and personalized gifts. A hobby project can also grow into custom work or a small business. Clawlab is set to unveil this smart knitting machine to a global audience at CES 2027.
The Engineering Foundation Behind Clawlab
Bringing professional knitting equipment into the home involves more than reducing its size. The real challenge is translating complex engineering into a product that feels intuitive to everyday users. Clawlab's founder and CEO Wenxin Hu previously worked as a hardware engineer at DJI and Meituan, while most members of the company's core R&D team are also former DJI employees. Together, they bring experience developing consumer-grade smart hardware and other technically complex products.
That background has shaped Clawlab's approach to product development. Rather than simply miniaturizing existing equipment or adding digital features, the company is rethinking the knitting experience across hardware, software, and interaction design around the needs of individual creators. The technology takes on the complexity, while users retain control of the creative process.
The Long-Term Vision in Knitting
Clawlab chose knitting based on a simple premise: textiles meet one of the most basic and enduring needs of everyday life.
"Textiles meet a broad, long-standing need in everyday life. Standardized products are abundant, but consumers' desire for personal style, customization, and emotional expression remains underserved," said Wenxin Hu. "We want to reconnect ideas, design, and production so that people without professional training can create through knitting."
Their longer-term ambition is to make knitting an everyday medium of expression. Smart knitting equipment, design software, and a creator community can help people turn ideas, memories, and care for others into one-of-a-kind pieces they can hold, share, and pass on.
About Clawlab
Clawlab is a technology startup founded in 2023 that develops smart tools for textile creation. It is building the future of knitting through a combination of innovative knitting technologies and a connected maker community. Its mission, "Push knitting forward. Bring more ideas to life," is to develop the tools and technology that help more people turn what they imagine into something they can hold. Clawlab's vision is to make knitting an everyday language for expression, much like words and pictures, through which people can tell their stories, preserve memories, and connect with others. For more information, please visit www.clawlab.com

SAN FRANCISCO , Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Delphina , whose Context Factory uses AI agents to build and maintain the business context behind trusted AI analytics, announced $7.5 million in new funding, bringing its total funding to $15 million. The round was co-led by Radical Ventures and Costanoa, with participation from Tenacity Capital joining high-profile angels Fei-Fei Li, Nobel laureate Guido Imbens, and early employees of Anthropic and OpenAI. . Delphina will use the funding to scale the Context Factory and grow its go-to-market and customer engineering teams.
Delphina was built to meet data teams' standards, but business teams now ask 73% of the questions on the platform, and CEOs at more than half of its customers are active users. At Substack, more than 70% of employees use Delphina, including CEO Chris Best. Other customers include LATAM Airlines, Gen Digital, Upstart, Udemy, Medely, Coursera, and BaseCamp Franchising.
"We want to give our people superpowers with AI. Delphina does that for data," said Chris Best, CEO of Substack. "Now our teams get accurate answers in seconds instead of waiting weeks in a queue. It's changed how we make decisions."
AI analytics is only as good as what it knows about the business: which tables are trusted, how metrics are defined, and what experienced analysts know but never wrote down. Most companies build that context by hand, and it goes stale as the business changes. The Context Factory hands that work to agents. They build a working baseline from a company's existing data and documents in hours, find and fix gaps as people ask questions, and route important changes to domain experts for approval.
"At Uber, everyone, including the CEO, was hands-on with data. That direct line to the numbers was a real advantage, but it took an army of data engineers to keep it from collapsing into chaos," said Jeremy Hermann, Delphina's CEO and co-founder. "The Context Factory gives every company that same advantage. Agents do the heavy lifting, and data teams become the knowledge captains who decide how the business sees its numbers."
"Most companies are data-obsessed but struggle to become data-driven," said Duncan Gilchrist, Delphina's President and co-founder. "When everyone can get trusted answers, everyone suddenly has questions. Ops, sales, marketing and finance teams are now the heaviest users of Delphina, and they keep coming back."
Hermann built and led Uber's Michelangelo machine learning platform and co-founded Tecton, which was acquired by Databricks. Gilchrist led global pricing data science at Uber. The Context Factory is available today at delphina.ai .

Delphina gives everyone in a company, from the front line to the CEO, trusted answers from the company's own data. Its Context Factory uses AI agents to build and maintain the business knowledge that enables accurate AI analytics, with experts approving important changes. Delphina is based in San Francisco and backed by Radical Ventures and Costanoa Ventures. Learn more at delphina.ai .
